**BILL NO. 1.658, 2011**
(From the Federal Senate)
**BILL NO. 43/2011**
**OFÍCIO Nº 1.206/2011** (SF)

Adds § 5 to Article 71 of the Consolidation of Labor Laws (CLT), approved by Decree-Law No. 5,452, of May 1, 1943, to provide for the collective negotiation of rest and meal intervals for employees driving and collecting fares in urban passenger collective transport, and provides for other measures.

The National Congress decrees:

**Article 1º O**

Article 71 of the Consolidation of Labor Laws (CLT), approved by Decree-Law No. 5,452, of May 1, 1943, is amended by adding the following § 5:

“Article 71. ...

...

§ 5º O The interval expressed in the first part may be fractioned, when it is comprised between the end of the first working hour and the beginning of the last working hour, provided that it is foreseen in a collective labor agreement or convention, in view of the nature of the service and in virtue of specific agreements between the categories involved.”

STATEMENT BY THE SPEAKER
Mr. President, Ladies and Gentlemen Deputies, I would like to present a brief report on the 100th International Labor Conference, held in Geneva, at which I had the honor of participating, by invitation of this House's Women's Caucus and UN Women.
After 18 days of intense debates and tripartite exchanges on the main issues on the agenda of the 100th International Labor Conference, the ILO successfully concluded the activities of one of the most important conferences in its history.

segments.text: DIARY OF THE HOUSE OF DEPUTIES

The Social Affairs Commission of the Senate held a public hearing on the last Tuesday to discuss the topic "Decent Work and Health of Railway Workers." Senator Paulo Paim proposed a series of debates focusing on various issues of interest to workers such as profession regulation; reduction of working hours and charges, collective bargaining and trade union freedom, work accidents, among others.

I sympathize with the situation. How do we know that approximately 13,000 railway workers, aged between 70 and 80, will lose the right to a health plan and be left high and dry? We need to consider the possibility of obtaining public funding to replenish the technical reserve and maintain the Railway Workers' Health Plan - PLANSFER in operation.

The representative of the National Federation of Railway Workers, João Edacir Calegari Morais, reminded that a solution to the case should be adopted in less than 30 days to prevent the closure of the railway workers' plan. After listening to the representatives of the railway workers, Paulo Paim announced that the Commission would provide full support to their claims. He stated that he would request a meeting with the Ministers of Labor, Carlos Lupi, and of Transport, Alfredo Nascimento, to address the issue. And at this moment, I take the opportunity to reinforce the appeal to the Ministers for the federal resources to be transferred to the railway workers' plan as soon as possible, as we cannot fail to recognize the importance of the railway family.

If we go back to the past, we can verify that the workers took pride in exercising this profession of railway worker. Indeed, one feels that there was a firm praise for work and an unparalleled spirit of teamwork. It can be said that this profession is in the DNA of the development of this country and that we need to honor these brave workers.

MR. WELLINGTON FAGUNDES (Block/PR-MT. Without revision of the speaker.) - Mr. President, initially, I would like to thank Deputy Mauro Benevides for this exchange, as I have to catch a flight this morning. I would like to put on record the work that the Ministry of Transport has been doing in our state, through Minister Alfredo Nascimento and also through comrade Luiz Antonio Pagot, Director-General of DNIT, who is from our state, with structural and extremely important works.

I would like to mention the duplication of the highway between Rondonópolis and Posto Gil, passing through Cuiabá, and the urban section of Lourencinho to the Police Highway, already under construction. This week, we also managed to obtain the environmental license for the duplication of the section from Posto Trevão to the future terminal of FER.

RONORTE, which will be the largest terminal of this railroad,
right in my state, in Rondonópolis, one of the central and important cities for agribusiness.
I also want to refer here to the Barra do Garças Ring Road, another extremely important work in the Araguaia region, which connects three cities, Barra do Garças, Pontal do Araguaia, and Aragarças, in Goiás. STATEMENT SENT BY THE SPEAKER
Mr. President, Ladies and Gentlemen Deputies, as everyone knows, Cuiabá will host one of the stages of the 2014 World Cup and, for this, it is expected to receive a large volume of investments in infrastructure works. I have advocated the idea that the World Cup should not only bring improvements to the Capital of Mato Grosso, but also to several others, such as Rondonópolis, located 210 kilometers south of Cuiabá. From Rondonópolis, it is possible to access one of the most preserved regions of the Mato Grosso Pantanal, not to mention other natural beauties. The city is emerging as a pole for agricultural production and cargo transport and will gain a new boost in its economy with the construction of the largest freight terminal of the Vicente Vuolo Railroad, which advances from Itiquira and whose tracks are expected to reach Rondonópolis by the end of 2012.

This week, I received the news of the approval, by the State Environmental Council, of the environmental license for the duplication of the track, asphalt paving, and drainage of the BR-163 section that will connect Rondonópolis to the freight terminal. The railroad connects the Central-West to the Port of Santos, in São Paulo.

In addition to the duplication of BR-163/364 between Rondonópolis – Cuiabá – Posto Gil, a total of 400 kilometers. The works are already underway in some sections, mainly between Posto Gil and the city of Rosário Oeste – a total of 44 kilometers – and in the São Vicente Mountains, where the asphalt is being replaced by concrete in two lanes. We also have urban crossings, such as in Rondonópolis, where the highway is being duplicated in a 14-kilometer section between the Federal Highway Police and the Lourencinho Creek.

With these infrastructure works, Rondonópolis will be more accessible to the tourist, who can also count on
DIARY OF THE HOUSE OF DEPUTIES

with a modern airport, whose expansion works were inaugurated last week. I have always worked on this project, concerned with meeting the logistical demand created by the region's development. The Municipal Airport Maestro Marinho Franco was built with resources from the National Aviation Fund. More recently, I managed to secure resources from the Ministry of Tourism for the expansion of the passenger terminal, in partnership with the Municipal Hall. With this, the airport gained space for the boarding room, access doors with metal detectors, restrooms and a diaper room, a disembarkation room with a rolling conveyor belt, space for commerce, a cafeteria and a central information counter. The work also contemplates the doubling of the number of airline counters and a location for the Federal Police. The resource also ensured the modernization of flight safety equipment.

The intention is to make this an airport of size comparable to that of Várzea Grande during periods of high passenger movement, such as, for example, during the 2014 World Cup season.

To make the project for building this airport a reality, I took a team from the Regional Air Command – COMAR to the city in 1997 for a hearing, where the need and possibility of building the new terminal were discussed.

With the approval of COMAR, the project for building a new, larger, better-equipped structure on a plot of land not so close to houses as was the case with the then José Salmen Hanse Airport began. At that time, Rondonópolis and the surrounding region received support from the Federal Government, which released resources, through the Federal Program for Airport Assistance – PROFAA, for the execution of the work.

Inaugurated in 2000, the new Maestro Marinho Franco Airport, equipped with night lighting, brought more tourists, businessmen and hope for the rescue of patients who needed to be transported for urgent treatment. New opportunities arrived through Rondonópolis's sky. The new structure attracted more passengers, who moved the location during boarding and disembarkation in daily flights to Cuiabá and other municipalities. The airport's operation was essential for the installation of companies such as Nortox, Petrópolis Brewery, as well as other ventures that move the economy and generate employment and income for hundreds of Rondonopolitan families.

Over the years and with the increase in passenger arrival and departure movement, the location became outdated and in need of improvements both in infrastructure and in the acquisition of equipment required by the National Civil Aviation Agency – ANAC.

segments.text:
Concerned about maintaining the development pace that the city is experiencing, I once again sought resources, and the expansion works were inaugurated last week.

I also want to record here another important work - but in another region of the state - the Barra do Garças Ring Road in the Araguaia region. This ring road will connect three cities: Barra do Garças, Pontal do Araguaia, and Aragarças, and two highways: BR-070 and BR-158. The bridges built over the Araguaia River date from the 1940s, and any problem that occurs ends up isolating the three cities. This ring road is, therefore, of extreme importance to the region, and I make an appeal to President Dilma to include this work in the Accelerating Growth Program - PAC.

I am aware, Mr. President, that there is still much to be done, and I will continue to dedicate myself to making Rondonópolis and Mato Grosso even better.

Thank you very much.

MR. MAURO BENEVIDES (PMDB-CE. Without revision by the speaker.) - Mr. President, during an audience with President José Sarney, the Presidents of Legislative Assemblies, among other just demands, claimed before the National Congress a rapid release regarding the creation of municipalities, a matter always postponed, leaving frustrated important political leaders from all federated units.

I also request the Head of the Legislative Power to adopt the claimed measures, putting in conditions of definition something of undeniable relevance to the fate of several districts that rightfully seek emancipation.

Since we are very close to the July recess, it is indispensable that we consensually adopt a position capable of resolving, without delays, this rumorous pending matter. That is why I could not remain silent in a debate that has now gained the indiscreet support of state legislators.

I believe that the leaders of the Chamber and the Senate, together, will assume the commitment to clarify this pulsating issue, adopting the legal parameters that can make the independence of the current conglomerates possible, many of which have over 30,000 inhabitants.

This is the appeal that I have decided to convey from this podium as a way to sensitize our eminent peers and those who make up the other House of Power to which we belong.

MR. RAIMUNDO GOMES DE MATOS (PSDB-CE. Without revision by the speaker.) - Mr. President, Ladies and Gentlemen Parliamentarians, the Diário do Nordeste newspaper, alongside the Ari de Sá Cavalcante College, is providing thousands of Ceará students with

On Thursdays, ENEM pamphlets are published, prepared by the teachers of Ari de Sá Cavalcanti School, which will guide students to achieve good performance in the tests. Our proposal is that it be spread throughout the country. (The microphone is turned off.)

STATEMENT BY THE SPEAKER

Mr. President, Ladies and Gentlemen, a partnership between the Northeast Daily newspaper and Ari de Sá Cavalcanti School will provide Ceará students with an important tool for good performance in the 2011 National High School Exam - ENEM. Out of a total of 16 pamphlets, accompanied by the newspaper every Thursday, the first one already reached students' hands on June 9th. This is the second consecutive year that the Northeast Daily acts in this segment, whose registrations for this year's ENEM edition reached approximately 230,000 only in Ceará.

Being one of the best-regarded schools in the state, Ari de Sá's teachers were responsible for elaborating questions in the exam model that will cover all relevant areas of the competition. This year, in addition to 180 questions and a composition, the novelty was the inclusion of a foreign language, with students able to choose between English or Spanish. As for the important partnership between the newspaper and the school, interested parties can check virtual simulations and video lessons with Ari de Sá's teachers, one day after the printed publication, who will be solving and commenting on main issues, as well as answering questions. At the end of the 16 pamphlets, a major simulation is scheduled for all students at Fortaleza University - UNIFOR.

Within the program, content on Composition and Languages, Codes and their Technologies will be published on June 16th, 23rd, and 30th, without mentioning the first one, which was launched on June 9th. Mathematics and its Technologies will be included on July 7th, 14th, 21st, and 28th. Human Sciences and their Technologies will be published on July 4th, 11th, 18th, and 25th.

on September 1st, 8th, 15th, and 22nd. It is important to note that all this material will reach the 184 municipalities of Ceará, democratizing quality education and contributing to the qualification of all young people.
Mr. President, Ladies and Gentlemen Deputies, created in 1998 by the Ministry of Education, the National High School Exam - ENEM revealed some weaknesses in 2009 and 2010. First, the leak of the test papers came to light, requiring last-minute cancellation, causing financial and psychological damage to the 4.1 million candidates in 1,800 cities across the country.
At the end of last year, another problem arose, involving printing errors on the test headers and repeated questions. In 2011, with the tests scheduled for October 23rd and 24th, we hope there will be more rigor in the preparation and distribution of ENEM tests.
Known as the Northeast Daily in ENEM, this project by the Northeast Daily and Ari de Sá could certainly be replicated across the country, and within public schools, contributing to the path of quality education. The Executive Director of the Ari de Sá Education System, Ari de Sá Neto, highlights the differentiated methodology from what is charged for university admission: "In this way, the project is an excellent opportunity to practice questions that involve greater contextualization."
Through the initiative of the Northeast Daily and Ari de Sá, we congratulate all those involved in this project.
That's all we had to say.
Mr. VALMIR ASSUNÇÃO (PT-BA. Without review by the speaker.) - Mr. President, Ladies and Gentlemen Deputies, I would like to make two notes.
First, to say that the teachers in the municipality of Casa Nova, Bahia, have been on strike for 44 days. After 44 days of camping in front of City Hall, they managed to negotiate with the Mayor, and the APLB emerged strengthened from this negotiation process. This was important for all teachers and, above all, for the students, as the demands were met, allowing for better quality education in that municipality.
The second note is to say that on the 25th, in Cachoeira, Bahia, the Government of Bahia will be installed, an event that is repeated every year in honor of those who fought for the independence of Bahia. The celebrations begin on July 2nd, the most important date for the state of Bahia and, above all, for Brazil, which culminated in the independence of our state and our country, Mr. President.
DIARY OF THE HOUSE OF DEPUTIES

Mr. President, Ladies and Gentlemen Deputies, after 44
days of stoppage, the teachers of the municipal network
of Casa Nova, Bahia, ended the strike and returned to
work last Thursday, June 16.
Organized by the Union of Education Workers of the
State of Bahia, APLB, and with broad support from several
other civil society organizations, the teachers had been
encampment on the lawn in front of the city hall as a
form of pressure on the local mayor to meet the demands
of the category.
The return was made after an agreement signed between
APLB/Union and the city mayor, in which he committed
to fulfill the demands for improvement of the working
conditions of educators and the structure of schools.
It cannot be said that the strike was not fair. In the
same way, it cannot be denied the effort that the
Municipal Administration, with all the difficulties inherent
to a small city, located in the semi-arid region, has made
to improve the conditions of public education.
Therefore, common sense prevailed, and teachers and
the municipality reached an agreement that ended the
strike, so that the student community would not be
further harmed.
Whoever knows the reality of the semi-arid region
knows the difficulties that teachers and students face
on a daily basis in schools. Despite the recovery work
done annually, physical conditions in schools of Casa
Nova are lacking, in addition to the scarcity of teaching
and pedagogical materials for classes. The lunch,
often, is not enough to meet the demand of students,
especially considering that for many, this constitutes
the only meal of the day. The same can be said of
school transport, which is done on rural roads that
become extremely difficult during rainy seasons. In
the case of Casa Nova, there is also the aggravating
factor that many students who live in the rural area
have to cross the São Francisco River by boat, to, on
the other side of the river, catch the bus that goes to
school. So, as we see, these are complex problems,
different from those that occur in large centers, but
which, in the agreement between teachers and the
Municipality, must be addressed.
The agreement that ended the strike contemplates
the national salary floor, the availability of 73 buses
for student transport within the Municipality, which
has one of the largest territorial extensions in Bahia,
and the reform of five schools starting from the next
recess in June/July 2011. By assuming these commitments,
Mayor Orlando Nunes guaranteed that he will
take the necessary measures to also resolve the problem
of the school in the Entroncamento community and
the resumption of the salary and position plan of the
category.

So, Ladies and Gentlemen Deputies, the strike by teachers and education professionals was legitimate. The situation is difficult for the class and also for the Municipality of Casa Nova. In the end, dialogue prevailed, which is what should govern all conflict situations.

I will now turn to another topic.
Mr. President, for the fourth consecutive year, the city of Cachoeira, 111 kilometers from Salvador, in the Baiano Recôncavo, will be the seat of the Government of Bahia. Governor Jaques Wagner is thus fulfilling what is provided for in Law 10.695, of 2007, approved by the Legislative Assembly of the State. The law stipulates that every year, on June 25th, the seat of the Government is to be installed in the Municipality. The act of transferring the seat of the Government also marks the official opening of the celebrations of July 2nd, the great date on which the Independence of Bahia is celebrated.

June 25th is also the great date for the city of Cachoeira, because in 1822, the Cachoeirans initiated the struggles for the Independence of Bahia, which culminated with July 2nd. In 2008, the city opened the seat of the Government for the first time. By adopting this procedure, Governor Jaques Wagner values not only our history, but pays an invaluable homage to the people of Cachoeira, who were the cradle where the ideals of liberation of Bahia from Portuguese rule were born and where the first concrete manifestations of the independence of the State emerged, which only occurred a year after the Act of Ipiranga, protagonized by Emperor D. Pedro I.

July 2nd is the most important date for Bahia and one of the most important for the Nation, as even after the declaration of independence in 1822, Brazil still needed to free itself from Portuguese troops that persisted in remaining in some Provinces. Therefore, for its importance, especially for the Bahians, every year Bahia celebrates July 2nd with the same enthusiasm as Brazilians celebrate September 7th.

It was in Cachoeira, this city of just over 32,000 inhabitants, bathed by the Paraguaçu River and inscribed as a National Historic Heritage, that on June 25, 1822, almost two months before the process of independence proclaimed by Emperor D. Pedro I, the people took the lead of the movement that ignited the war for the independence of Bahia. The Cachoeirans reacted to the attacks of a troop of Portuguese military, on board a Lusitanian cannonboat anchored in the Paraguaçu River, which tried to besiege the village with the aim of suppressing the popular mobilization against colonial domination.

On that same June 25, 1822, the Councillors of Cachoeira drafted a minute acclamating D. Pedro de Alcântara, Perpetual Regent of Brazil. With this, they declared that from that day on, the city would be free territory from Portuguese domination. Thus, it was declared that...
DIARY OF THE HOUSE OF DEPUTIES

Caught in the first concrete act of our independence,
which, despite being a pioneer in Brazil, only consolidated in Bahia a year later, on July 2, 1823.
That is why the date is considered a milestone for the Bahians.
To reach today's day, free and sovereign, the Brazilians, and the Bahians in particular, had to wage many battles. But the struggle of the Bahians for freedom had the effective participation of indigenous peoples, symbolically identified as the true Brazilians, the owners of the land, and the miscigenated peoples with still enslaved blacks, who joined their efforts to other combatants. That is why, in the celebrations of July 2, in addition to civic and military rites, we have the figures of the Indians and the caboclo and cabocla.
We know, Ladies and Gentlemen Deputies, that the process of a people's independence does not consolidate merely through decrees. One hundred and eighty-eight years later, Bahia consolidated its independence with a democratically elected government that meets the interests of the population. This is because, unlike the rest of the country, we have lived under the rule of tyranny for the past 40 years, until the victory of democratic forces represented by Governor Jacques Wagner and his entire support base, due to oligarchies that insisted on keeping Bahia in backwardness in terms of freedom of expression and the free manifestation of its people.
But just as the Bahians of 1823, the Bahians of today said no to tyranny and elected as their leader a democratic government. They also participate in this democratic government that they themselves chose. They consolidate independence in the manifestations of social movements such as the black, the landless, indigenous peoples, those of African-based religions, and the LGBT people. And they say no to any process of tyranny that threatens to take away this freedom so hard-won.
That is why here I want not only to congratulate the Bahian people on this date, and particularly the people of Cachoeira, for their invaluable contribution to our independence, but also Governor Jacques Wagner, who, with the gesture of transferring the seat of government to the city of Cachoeira, pays tribute to a people that fought so hard for us to live in full democracy today.

Mr. President, Ladies and Gentlemen Deputies, even though regional disparities remain stark, Brazil became less unequal in the last decade, thanks to Bolsa Família, according to data released by the demographic census of IBGE, in the newspaper Folha de S.Paulo, on Sunday, June 19. The report delved into how the movement affected cities throughout northeastern Brazil.

Northeastern cities led the gains in per capita income, and those in São Paulo made the least progress. Among the 50 municipalities with over 100,000 inhabitants that advanced the most in this regard, between 2000 and 2010, half are in the Northeast, and only one is in São Paulo. The newspaper states that, according to experts, the increase in the minimum wage and Bolsa Família help explain the reduction in disparities over the last decade.

Between 2000 and 2010, average income rose 3% in São Paulo cities and 46% in Maranhão cities.

Note that disparities persist, however. It is recorded that over the last 14 years, 73% of Brazilian families have changed their social class due to increased income, a contingent of 143 million people. This is a mobility superior to that seen in the United States, Sweden, and Canada over such a short period of time. The data is from a survey by IPC Maps Consulting.

Already on the list of the 50 that advanced the least, 36 are from São Paulo. Correcting 2000 values by the cumulative inflation over 10 years by INPC (IBGE's indicator), 12 even experienced a slight decline in average income. Nine of them are from São Paulo.

It is natural that poorer municipalities have greater room for advancement. However, this is not always the case in a country accustomed to inequality. In the 1980s, for example, São Paulo saw the average income of its households rise 17%, while Maranhão advanced 7%.

In the last decade, São Paulo households recorded the smallest growth among all Federal Units (just 3%), while Maranhão's variation was 46%.

Without revision of the speaker.) – Mr. President, Ladies and Gentlemen Deputies, I request that the statement I am about to deliver be considered as read, in which I express our disappointment that the 2011/2012 Crop Plan, announced by the Federal Government last week, does not contain any reference to the Disaster Fund. This House, the National Congress as a whole, has approved over several years all the necessary regulations for the implementation of this fund, which will mitigate the suffering of rural producers who work outdoors in a high-risk activity. We have built all the legislative framework for this, including breaking the monopoly of reinsurance in Brazil. However, unfortunately, it has not yet been regulated, and the decree that should resolve this situation, unfortunately, will not meet the needs of this crop.

STATEMENT DELIVERED BY THE SPEAKER
Mr. President, Ladies and Gentlemen Deputies, last week the Government launched the 2011/2012 Crop Plan. In my view, the Federal Government missed the opportunity to regulate the Disaster Fund. The law that created the Fund was sanctioned by the President of the Republic last August with the promise to apply 4 billion reais through public securities. However, to this day, almost a year later, the Government has not made the regulation, which, in practice, renders ineffective all the effort of the Congress in the discussion of this important legal instrument.

Worse: rural producers will once again face a crop, assuming all the risks inherent to their activity. I am well acquainted with the dilemmas of Brazilian rural producers. A rural property is a business open to the sky, subject to rains, droughts, and all kinds of weather conditions. The regulation of the law will bring more security to farmers in times of adverse climatic events. Therefore, this delay is unacceptable, considering that the Legislature has worked for several years to remove an endless series of difficulties, and rural producers are disappointed with this decision, as they expected to count on the protection of the Fund for this year's crop.

It is worth noting that this sector accounts for a significant portion of the national GDP, but it is the only one to bear all the risks inherent to its activities. I believe that it is the role of the Government to create support mechanisms for agriculture, such as the Disaster Fund.

The main objective of the Disaster Fund is to make agricultural insurance viable through the creation of a private consortium composed of insurance companies and reinsurers, which would benefit from Federal Government subsidies. The consortium would be responsible for management and coverage.

Without a speaker’s review.) – Mr. President, ladies and gentlemen Members, the press throughout Brazil reported yesterday that the international credit rating agency Moody’s raised Brazil’s rating for public Treasury securities. From now on, securities issued by the National Treasury will be considered safe investments by major global financial capitalists.

There was celebration by the Government and its support base in Congress, but I wish to disagree with this celebration here.

International credit rating agencies are today institutions under suspicion, because after the international financial crisis of 2008 and 2009, and especially after the crisis that began in Ireland, these agencies got it wrong. Most of them certified the solidity of North American financial operations, of residential mortgages, of the Irish financial system, but the crisis that began in these countries affected the entire world.

It is a shame that agencies paid to defend the interests of speculators come to our country and tell us what to do, as the Moody’s representative did, who, last week, in an interview with the Valor Econômico newspaper, stated that he was concerned about the fact that in Brazil, the minimum wage is linked to the payment of Social Security benefits, and that we should decouple the payment of Social Security benefits from the actual value of the minimum wage.

Moreover, Mr. President, ladies and gentlemen Members, the higher the appreciation of public securities, the more speculative foreign investment will come to the country. And then, what will the Central Bank do? Will it intervene in the foreign exchange market, buy dollars, and issue public securities to take out of circulation the Brazilian currency, used to buy these dollars, thereby increasing public debt.

Therefore, as a PDT Deputy who defends national sovereignty, I wish to express my rejection of the great space, the red carpet that much of the national media has given to this credit rating agency.

Brazil does not have to worry about transforming itself into a paradise for short-term speculation. Brazil has to worry about applying its fiscal savings to technological innovation, raising educational levels, increasing the number of masters and doctors.

MR. MENDONÇA FILHO (DEM-PE and as Leader. Without revision by the speaker.) – Mr. President, Ladies and Gentlemen Parliamentarians, I occupy the tribune of the Chamber of Deputies this morning to speak about some matters that concern the interests of Brazil.

I begin my speech by commenting on an international episode that unfortunately affects our country, on which, in my view, the Brazilian Government, which should adopt a harder, clearer, and more effective position, has been silent. I am referring specifically to the decision of the President of Bolivia, Mr. Evo Morales, to, through a presidential decree, legalize vehicles circulating in that country, which, in the vast majority, were stolen in the countries that make up the MERCOSUR – Argentina, Paraguay, Uruguay, and particularly Brazil – and Chile.

This measure taken by President Morales and recently published is, in my opinion, absurd and mistaken. It has outraged a large part of the Brazilian population because, on the one hand, there will be a certain market for the commercialization of stolen vehicles within our territory; on the other, it will impose an additional financial burden on the Brazilian society.

Everyone knows that the cost of insurance in Brazil is defined, among other factors, based on risk. Therefore, theft is certainly the factor that most increases the cost of a vehicle insurance in our territory.

Well, with the decision of the Bolivian Government and
the Brazilian Government to legalize stolen cars within our territory and circulating in that country,
it will obviously be much easier for thieves to steal cars on our territory to sell in Bolivia, as they will be sure of a market.
Unfortunately, until now I have not heard, read, or accompanied a single position from the Brazilian Government. Itamaraty remains silent, the Ministry of Justice also does not speak, and society watches in amazement as this episode unfolds, with developments that, in fact, only depict an attempt to deceive.
The Bolivian Government recently stated that it will analyze the RENAVAM registration of the countries that make up the MERCOSUR directly affected by the measure, including Brazil, to compare the registration of vehicles that will be legalized under the adopted measure.
In fact, Ladies and Gentlemen Parliamentarians, this is only an attempt to deceive the general public and the Brazilian population. It is known that in the year 2010, according to statistics from the National Federation of Private Insurance Companies and Capitalization, approximately 400,000 vehicles were stolen on Brazilian territory, 50% of which were recovered.
With this decision adopted by the Bolivian Government, certainly the indicators of car theft on Brazilian territory will rise. Indeed, Mr. President, Ladies and Gentlemen Parliamentarians, I have news that the price of car insurance, particularly in states like Mato Grosso do Sul, is already beginning to rise due to this reality.
So, I make an appeal from this House of the National Congress for the government authorities, the Minister of Foreign Affairs, and the Minister of Justice to speak up in defense of the Brazilian population, not cower or mince words, as the former President Lula would say.
Even from poor countries—I have total respect for the Bolivian people—, we cannot accept this type of conduct. By the way, the current President of Bolivia, Mr. Evo Morales, is a repeat offender. He committed an act of insult to Brazilian sovereignty when he invaded and occupied the oil refinery belonging to PETROBRAS in that country without any adequate reaction from the Brazilian Government.
Therefore, I leave this record. We have submitted a request, likely to be considered next week—starting with the word of President Marco Maia—to send a motion of reproach and we can express our opinion about this mistaken decision adopted by the Bolivian Government, through President Evo Morales.

Mr. Atila Lins (PMDB-AM. No speaker's review.) - Mr. President, Ladies and Gentlemen Deputies, I would like to request the insertion, in the records of this House, of an editorial published by Folha de S.Paulo last Monday regarding the salaries of the Military Police, Civil Police, and Military Firemen in the country.

This editorial, Mr. President, clearly illustrates the true meaning of PEC 300. There was misinformation on the part of the Planning Ministry at the time we approved PEC 300 in first round, that the establishment of a minimum salary for the Military Police, Civil Police, and Military Firemen would cause a 45 billion real hole in public accounts.

In fact, Mr. President, PEC 300 does not fix any value for the salary or minimum salary of military, civil, and firemen police officers. What PEC 300 does is create a minimum salary for these categories and stipulates that, within 180 days, the Executive Power shall present to this House a complementary law establishing the value of the minimum salary created by the Constitutional Amendment Proposal.

Now, if there is no value in the constitutional amendment, and the President has not yet sent a complementary law stating what the minimum salary is, how can one calculate that there will be a hole in public accounts of any value if there is no fixed value for the minimum salary yet?

Folha de S.Paulo depicts the matter with fidelity, stating that, at first, we intended to fix the minimum salary at the same values as what the Police earns in Brasília, but later we evolved, because the Constitution does not allow the linking of values, of employment, of position, or of salary. So, we considered the value of 3,500 reals, since the salary of the Military Police in Brasília is 4,500 reals. Finally, we understood that we should not fix any value, leaving it to the Executive Power, after extensive negotiations with the State Governors, to fix a value, and perhaps, within a period of 1 to 2 years, reach the ideal, which would be 3,500 reals for the minimum salary of a Military Police soldier at the beginning of his career, of the Civil Police, and of the Military Firemen.

Therefore, Mr. President, I request that you record in the records the editorial of Folha de S.Paulo, because, in fact, we want PEC 300 to be approved in second round and that, afterward, the value of the minimum salary be negotiated, so as not to let the crisis that started in Rio de Janeiro with the Military Firemen spread throughout the country.

Thank you very much.

Loan from BNDES, taking money from the poor, education, health, social policies, minimum wage, to transfer to a select and small group of companies that access subsidized interest rates. Industrial policy, BNDES and budgetary priorities
Who has R$ 270 billion to buy government bonds?

Wednesday, June 8, 9 PM. The Chamber of Deputies rejected the motion of reproach regarding President Dilma's failure to receive Iranian lawyer Shirin Ebadi, Nobel Peace Prize winner in 2003. Over 360 deputies voted.

At 9:30 PM, the provisional measure No. 526/2011 was discussed. There were no more than ten deputies in the chamber.

The day had been long. At the meeting installed at 2 PM, everything and more was discussed. At the moment when the most important issue was to be discussed, there were less than ten deputies in the chamber.

On behalf of the PSDB, I took the floor. I revealed my astonishment at the emptying of the chamber while we were to debate the transfer of R$ 55 billion from the Union budget so that BNDES could continue the Investment Support Program (PSI), carrying out highly subsidized credit operations, particularly for large companies.

The role of the National Congress is to make good laws, just laws. Laws that carry the values of equity, justice, and freedom. That is not the case with MP 526.

Secondary aspects of the MP are positive: subsidized credit for producers and companies affected by natural disasters and favorable norms for philanthropic hospitals.

But the essence is absurd. What is at stake? A brutal transfer of income and an inversion of priorities, taking money from public health, education, and social policies to finance the difference between the government's capture rate (Selic at 12.25%) and the PSI loan rates (TJLP around 5% to 8%). As Milton Friedman said, "There is no free lunch," and as public finance managers affirm, "Money does not have a stamp." With these authorized R$ 55 billion, we will reach the astronomical

The figure of R$ 270 billion injected into BNDES. Money
from the taxpayer that could have alternative applications.
In times of depression, it would justify itself as an anti-cyclical policy. But the Brazilian economy experienced a 7.5% GDP growth in 2010.
The credit operations are extremely concentrated. 72% of the operations focus on large companies. Only 13% of the credits went to micro and small businesses.
At the end of my statement, I pointed out two issues. First, who has R$ 270 billion to buy government bonds? Wouldn't the same economic agents be benefiting double: at the tip, from subsidized credit, and on the other side, from speculation, enjoying the highest real interest rate? Wouldn't that be the old financial circle? Second, why doesn't the investment rate keep pace with the GDP growth rate?
Intent and action do not always walk hand in hand. Rhetoric is one thing, reality is another. The PT has been generous with large companies, even sacrificing substantial resources that could improve health, education, and the minimum wage.

The values listed in the table of the Association of Private Hospital Doctors of the Federal District - AMHP are around 50 reais per consultation, with the patient's return already included in this value. Mr. President, we understand that the user pays for their plan and needs good service, but the amounts paid by health plan operators to doctors and other professionals should be discussed and adjusted. According to Cid Carvalhaes, President of the National Federation of Doctors, the abusive relationship to which healthcare professionals are exposed leads the category to consider mass disenrollment, and if they haven't done so yet, it's because they think about the public interest of Brazilians and Brazilian women seeking healthcare.

STATEMENT DELIVERED BY THE SPEAKER
Mr. President, ladies and gentlemen, I come to the podium of this House to speak about overcoming poverty in Brazil, in both rural and urban areas.
In the Brazilian context of the past 8 years, overcoming poverty has been an imperative adopted during the Lula government, and it has also been one of the priorities of the Dilma Rousseff government. The launch of the Brazil Without Poverty Plan on June 2nd materializes one of the campaign priorities of the current President, and it also makes real a political option of commitment to the poorest. Raising income levels, in the light of expanding and guaranteeing social rights, contributes to changing the social structure of the country.
Bringing the public debate on overcoming poverty to the forefront allows millions of Brazilians, who have been excluded from citizenship due to latent poverty that afflicts their lives, to come out of the shadows. According to current data from the Ministry of Social Development and Hunger Combat (MDS), in recent years, 28 million people have been lifted out of poverty, and 36 million have entered the middle class. In this regard, the debate around the topic of poverty involves a series of elements, given its multidimensional nature.
It is also important to remember that this debate brings with it the discussion of the ongoing development project in Brazilian society, linked to high rates of social mobility and the model of social protection adopted in Brazil.
However, before delving into these issues, I will begin by highlighting the history of our country, with the intention of showing that poverty transcends the condition of a recent phenomenon, has a structural base resulting from the very functioning and contradictions of capitalism, and involves, above all, a historical dimension that singularizes its characteristics in Brazilian society.
Throughout the history of Brazilian society, poverty has revealed itself as an inescapable and persistent reality in the face of a nation that was already tutelated under the signs of the white colonizer and of European origin. The exploitation of indigenous and African slave labor is a real constituent of voluntary servitude that permeated the primordia

Under the English regime, it bears traits that mix the universality and impersonality of laws with hierarchical practices constructed by the universe of personal relations.

It is commonly argued that there was an inversion in the chronology described by Marshall about the course of Brazilian citizenship. Social rights were the first rights established in Brazil, especially during Vargas' government in 1930; then, political rights were established, and finally, civil rights. However, this order of rights was constituted through immense contradictions, given the consolidation of power in Brazil.

In this trajectory, the consolidation of social rights in Brazil has a direct relationship with the roots of historical processes marked by conservative and authoritarian characteristics. Patriarchalism and mandonism, typical practices of the plantation owners in the Brazilian Colony and later of the coffee plantation owners, are also part of a Brazilian heritage that ratifies the place of the destitute within a hierarchy of natural order, where authoritarianism was the measure of civility. Those devoid of court privileges had the duty of obedience.

As Vera Telles (2006) states, the Brazilian society carries the weight of a country with a slave past and that entered capitalism's modern era within a patriarchal conception of command and authority, a conception that translates differences and inequalities in the record of hierarchies that create the figure of the inferior who has the duty to obey, who deserves favor and protection, rather than rights.

In Brazil, during the transition from the 19th to the 20th century, poverty manifested as a sign of backwardness in a society that proclaimed ideas of progress, the economic growth of the coffee agro-export sector, the abolition of slavery, industrial modernity, and the urbanization process. However, the ideals of modernity proclaimed by the Republic, under the positivist paths of order and progress, became timid in the context of local oligarchies.

During the Republic of the Coronels, as the First Republic became known, the loyalty exercised by citizens towards the local chief was predominantly personal, given the strong power of the oligarchies of the large states, especially São Paulo and Minas Gerais.

Urban poverty, depicted in courtyards and new modes of being of free but poor workers, became a concern of the elites. It was necessary to sanitize or even moralize this class laden with so many negative adjectives.

Another important trait in the constitution of Brazilian citizenship refers to the interrelationship between citizenship and class.

The relationship between citizenship and work. Being a citizen should be directly linked to the condition of a worker, integrated into a corporate contractual logic. Roberto DaMatta (1997), citing the famous expression "regulated citizenship" by Wanderley Guilherme dos Santos, ratifies a citizenship that is somewhat upside down, recognized and defined as a law granted by the state and linked to an occupational stratification system, not to a code of political values. Thus, some categories, generally linked to the general idea of a worker, acquired more rights than others.

Therefore, as Vera Teles (2006) reports, the labor card in the 1930s was the certificate of civic belonging. The law, instead of guaranteeing and universalizing rights, deprived individuals of their citizenship privileges and created a fracture between the figure of the worker and that of the uncivil poor. The state's social protection system, of a corporate nature, was aimed at workers integrated into the labor market.

Thus, it is evident that social protection, at that time, under the logic of social security, was intended for individuals regularly circumscribed in the labor market. And those who, being part of the productive sector, were unable to work due to some vicissitude of life, such as illness and disability. Those who escaped the rules of the contract were destined for social assistance actions, at the time still linked to charity and help for the poor.

Based on these historical foundations and deep social inequalities, pauperization manifested itself throughout Brazil's historical trajectory in the record of excessive poverty.

One of the milestones in the recent history of the manifestation of the defense of social rights in Brazil was the democratic experiences lived in the 1980s in the country. Emerging from a still repressive scenario, given the military dictatorship period, collective resistance movements emerged against the culture of fear and obedience to uniforms.

The emergence of new social movements in Brazil from the 1980s, such as popular base movements, like the urban social movements (CEBs - Basic Christian Communities, Church Base Communities), the strengthening of new urban and later rural trade unions, the feminist movement, the ecological movement, among others, gave strength to the consolidation of new democratic experiences in the political arena.

The legal guarantee of civil and political rights acquired in the 1988 Citizen Constitution revealed signs of redimensioning of the public sphere, the expansion of participatory processes between the state and civil society, the principles of universalization and democratic management.

It is emphasized that the consolidation of rights and, consequently, the realization of citizenship in any society passes, without fail, through the guarantees of social relationship regulation, inscribed in laws and institutions. However, although the importance of legal mechanisms is recognized, the analysis is focused on the relationship established between social rights, citizenship, and societal dynamics, or the social practices constructed through the specificities of Brazil's historical and cultural processes.

It must be remembered that, in the economic sphere, the 1980s are considered the "lost decade," as there is an exhaustion of the Brazilian miracle, based on the import substitution model and the autocratic bourgeois development policy of the military dictatorship.

Among the factors that characterize the economic crisis that plunges the country into the 1980s, the following stand out: profound external indebtedness due to the reorientation of U.S. economic policy in pursuit of dollar hegemony; high interest rates; reduction in investment rates and recrudescence of inflation.

According to Elaine Behring and Ivanete Boschetti (2010), Brazil jumped from an annual inflation rate of 91.2% to 217.9% in 1985. The effects of the debt crisis were significant: generalized poverty in Latin America, a crisis in public social services, unemployment, increased informal work, and favoritism towards export-oriented production at the expense of internal needs.

Thus, Brazil ends the 1980s mired in high inflationary processes and the failures of economic plans, in addition to increased external debt. In the face of the possibility of financial collapse, neoliberal discourse fits perfectly into Brazilian society, especially in the 1990s.

Guided by the formulations of international institutions and as a way to contain the established crisis, fiscal adjustment policies are introduced, coupled with reductions in social spending in public policies, as a means of promoting economic stabilization. During this period, there is a reevaluation of the achievements of 1988. The reforms announced by the Collor government and implemented by the FHC government dismantled the Brazilian state, making the country available to the market, particularly to financial market speculators.

According to authors Elaine Behring and Ivanete Boschetti (2010), privatization processes in Brazil delivered a significant portion of public wealth to foreign capital. However, it is noticed that from 2000 to 2010, especially under the Lula government, new issues are brought to the forefront. The priority given to tackling poverty and the changes observed around social security policies, particularly social assistance, are significant in the debate.

The 1988 Constitution expanded social rights and the field of social protection under state responsibility, with significant impacts on policy design, user definition, and benefits. According to Luciana Jaccoud (2009), from the 1990s, especially from 2000 to 2010, the Brazilian state began operating with a broader range of social policies, addressing social problems that emerged on the public agenda.

Examples include: the Food and Nutritional Security Policy; the Eradication of Child Labor Program; the Bolsa Família Program; the institutionalization of the National Policy on Social Assistance, approved at the deliberations of the IV Social Assistance Conference, held in December 2003 in Brasília; and the consolidation of the Basic Operational Norm that implements the Single System of Social Assistance (NOB/SUAS/2005), by the National Council on Social Assistance. These public policies and programs have significant impacts on the lives of the poorest and most vulnerable segments, who are socially unprotected.

During the Lula government, the implementation of the Bolsa Família Program unified the various income transfer programs existing in Brazil, such as Bolsa Escola, Bolsa Alimentação, Vale Gás, and Cartão Alimentação. This program is characterized by direct income transfer actions with conditions, benefiting families in situations of poverty and extreme poverty.

The program integrates the Zero Hunger Program, which aims to ensure the human right to adequate food, promoting food and nutritional security, and contributing to the achievement of citizenship by the most vulnerable population to hunger.

The Bolsa Família Program is structured around three main axes: income transfer, conditions, and complementary programs. Income transfer provides immediate relief from poverty. Conditions reinforce access to basic social rights in the areas of education, health, and social assistance. Complementary programs aim to develop families, so that beneficiaries can overcome their vulnerability situation.

The program serves over 12 million families across the national territory. Depending on income

Familiar per person, limited to R$140.00, based on the number and age of children, the benefit received by the family can range from R$32.00 to R$242.00. These values are the result of the adjustment announced on March 1st of this year and apply to benefits paid in April 2011.

The obligation for beneficiaries to access conditions, such as the enrollment and attendance of children and adolescents of school age in the education network, the monitoring of children's vaccination schedules, and the provision of prenatal care for pregnant women, aims to build an intersectoral perspective among public policies.

In addition, the program provides access to basic social services of social assistance, as most beneficiary families of the PBF reside in the territories of the Centers of Reference for Social Assistance - CRAS. Identifying, monitoring, and referring these families to programs, projects, and services of the Social Protection Network through CRAS strengthens the articulation of this program with other public policies, as well as favors the construction of autonomy of these subjects beyond just receiving the benefit.

The management of Bolsa Família is decentralized and shared among the Union, States, Federal District, and Municipalities.

This process stands out for the profound changes in positions of distinct population segments within the social structure. According to Marcio Pochmann (2010), based on data from IBGE, between 2003 and 2008, the average family income at the distribution base of the 10% poorest grew, on average, 9.1% per year, while the average per capita family income of the 10% richest grew by 1.6%, on average. This is due to the policy of increasing the real minimum wage, which allowed an injection of R$1 trillion into the incomes of low-wage workers only in the period from 2003 to 2010. Another data revealing the increase in the income of the poorest is due to the policy of transferring income to the most vulnerable segments. Through Social Security, especially with the Continuous Performance Benefit - BPC, or through social assistance through the Bolsa Família Program, among others.

According to Pochmann (2010), between 2002 and 2008, for example, the transfer of income to the most vulnerable segments of the population was at least multiplied by 2.3 times, from R$134.7 billion to R$305.3 billion.

Thus, at the beginning of this millennium, one witnesses the combination of the continuity of monetary stability, economic growth concomitant with the real increase in the minimum wage value, and the reformulation and expansion of social protection policies.

gaining from income transfer programs. However, all these positive factors are still combined with the existence of extreme poverty in a large part of the Brazilian society. In Brazil, according to the last IBGE census data from 2010: 16.27 million Brazilians, or 8.5% of the total population, live in extreme poverty in Brazil; 59% are concentrated in the Northeast Region - 9.6 million people; of the total Brazilians in rural areas, 46.7% are extremely poor; 53.3% are in urban areas; 50.9% are aged up to 19 years old; 39.9% are aged up to 14 years old; 50.5% are extremely poor women and 49.5% are men; 53% of households are not connected to the general sewage network or septic tank; 48% of poor households are not connected to the general water distribution network and do not have a well or spring on the property; 70.8% are black - black and brown; 26% are illiterate - 15 years or older. It is worth emphasizing that the largest contingent of Brazilians living in extreme poverty is concentrated in the Northeast (18.1%) and North (16.8%) regions. Of every 100 Brazilian citizens living in extreme poverty,
75 reside in one of these two Regions. From these data, it becomes evident that the face of
Brazilian poverty carries with it multiple dimensions,
such as urban and rural poverty. In addition to other
characteristics that deepen class asymmetries, like generation, gender, race/ethnicity marks. Thus, besides income indicators that define poverty lines related to the achievement
of basic survival needs, poverty is aggravated by the
historical discrimination legacy of some socially ex-
cluded groups, directly worsening the universality of
human rights. According to Sônia Rocha (2005), a recurrent
discussion specifically regarding income as the main
variable for measuring poverty refers to the determina-
tion of poverty lines. Studies on poverty lines set a monetary
value crossed with the expenditure for meeting the
needs of a person, according to the parameters of the
total population divided into two subgroups, based on
the poverty and indigence lines, using income as the
criterion. According to Rocha (2005), the poor are those unable to meet the minimum needs of that society. The indigent, on the other hand, are a subset of the poor whose income is insufficient to cover only nutritional needs. The indigence line is associated with spending on food, while the poverty line relates to the value necessary to meet vital needs that go beyond food, such as clothing.

In this sense, family consumption is the most appropriate source for establishing poverty lines. The author, on the other hand, advocates the need to use two complementary concepts to analyze poverty: income and basic needs, especially in comparisons of reality between countries. The complexity of this phenomenon and its specificities in diverse contexts make it difficult to establish universal parameters.

According to Sônia Rocha (2005), absolute poverty, therefore, refers to issues of physical survival, the failure to meet needs linked to the vital minimum. Relative poverty defines the needs to be satisfied, based on the predominant way of life in the society in question, which means incorporating the reduction of inequalities. It consequently implies delimiting a set of relatively poor individuals in societies where the vital minimum is already guaranteed to all.

Relative poverty brings with it the discussion about social inequalities, due to international comparisons between countries. Beyond the criterion of income, the debate about relative poverty addresses issues linked to distributive justice, considering the specificity of each country's socio-economic and cultural development.

In this sense, it aligns with the debate on poverty as a lack of income, the absence and/or precariousness of conditions for access to public policies, such as education, health, housing, sanitation, insufficient access to the labor market concomitantly with the guarantee of social security policies, access to land, as well as a low level of political and civic consciousness.

The Indian economist Amartya Sen (2000) reports that to identify poverty, one should consider the criterion of low income, but needs to extrapolate it, as it also results from the deprivation of capabilities. He reports that there are several reasons that should be taken into account, especially in public action aimed at reducing inequality and poverty.

According to Sen, the relationship between income and capability would be acutely affected by a person's age, given the specific needs of the elderly; by sexual and social roles, for example, the historical responsibilities of women with regard to motherhood and also family obligations; by location and epidemiological conditions.

This conception has influenced some international organizations in their understandings of the topic. According to Vivian Ugá (2004), the World Bank reports from the period 2000-2001 differ from the reports of 1990. In the 1990 report, poverty consisted of the inability to achieve a certain level of income.

Minimum living standard, which should be evaluated by consumption, that is, the necessary expense to acquire a minimum nutritional standard and other basic needs, and still allow the person's participation in the daily life of society. In the World Bank report for 2000 and 2001, poverty is analyzed as a multifaceted phenomenon resulting from multiple deprivations produced by economic, political, and social processes that interact with each other. According to this World Bank report, the state should intervene to increase the human capabilities of the poor, since development, according to Sen, is seen as a process of expansion of freedoms. According to authors Pierre Salama and Blandine Destremau (1999), the elaborations of the UNDP, the United Nations Development Program, are also based on the theoretical inspirations of Amartya Sen. The production/reproduction of poverty takes into account all aspects of the economic, social, and political life of the poor, as well as issues of identity, social position, and representations. Human development for the UNDP is a process aimed at expanding the possibilities offered to individuals. These possibilities are infinite and evolve over time, highlighting: the possibility of leading a long and healthy life, the acquisition of knowledge, and access to necessary resources to have a decent standard of living. According to the UNDP, poverty can mean more than the absence of what is necessary for material well-being, also being the denial of opportunities and the possibilities of essential choices for human development. Based on these understandings of poverty by these two international organizations, some considerations should be made. First, these poverty concepts are centered on the absence of individual incapacity of individuals. Thus, the poor would be the incapable individuals who cannot ensure their survival, especially through insertion in the labor market. Second, by focusing on the poor, the role of the state would be to remove these people from this incapacity condition to insert them into the market, reinforcing their human capabilities. The very configuration of the state is questioned from this notion, especially in the context of the Brazilian history as narrated above, where the absence of a sense of citizenship is still possible in the Brazilian reality, therefore, this poverty notion must be properly considered according to the sociopolitical characteristics of each country. The fundamental role of the state is to guarantee policies

public policies that are articulated and universal. Compensatory and income transfer policies are fundamental for immediate income guarantees for those completely devoid of minimal survival conditions. However, articulation with broad and universal protection policies is fundamental for the consolidation of social rights. The poor cannot be solely blamed and stigmatized for a living condition that surpasses their individual desires, given the economic and social structure in which they are embedded. Author Carmelita Yasbeck (1996) warns of the need not to consider poverty only as an economic category, as it is not expressed solely by income insufficiency and lack of material goods, but also as a political category, translating into a lack of rights, opportunities, and hope. It reaches the spiritual, moral, and political plane of individuals facing survival problems. Brazilian poverty constitutes a heterogeneous field, whose unity is sought in limited income, exclusion, and subalternity. Thus, overcoming poverty requires direct income transfer programs to the poorest, in addition to other universal public policies and economic growth. The importance of expanding and redefining the Bolsa Família program to lower-income segments is recognized. Data from IPEA (2010) reveals that in Brazil, the monthly per capita family income of beneficiary families increases by 48.74% after receiving program benefits. Due to regional inequalities and the concentration of families in poverty, in the Northeast this income grows by 62.93%. Other initiatives adopted from the Lula government, such as raising the minimum wage, expanding popular credit, and supporting initiatives of the organized civil society to generate employment and income, such as solidary economy, were fundamental to reducing poverty and social inequalities in Brazil. For the years 2004-2010, the minimum wage had an average annual real value increase of 7.1% due to the policy of valuing the minimum wage agreed with the workers' movements, starting in 2007. This implies numerous factors that
contemplate the improvement of the quality of life of formal workers, retirees and pensioners,
as well as stimulating the country's economy. Regarding popular credit policies, stand out rural credit policies, mainly for family farming. The National Program for the Strengthening of Family Farming - PRONAF finances individual or collective projects that generate income for

Family farmers and settlers of agrarian reform. The program has the lowest interest rates for rural financing and the lowest default rates among the country's credit systems. In addition to the conventional PRONAF financing forms, which vary according to the financed limit, PRONAF has specific lines. Each of these aims to meet the specific needs of the target audience.

Highlight the specific PRONAF Semi-Arid lines, which finance investments in projects for living with the semi-arid region, focusing on the sustainability of agroecosystems, prioritizing water infrastructure and its implementation, expansion, recovery or modernization of other infrastructures, including those related to agro-pecuary and non-agro-pecuary production and service projects, according to the reality of farmer families in the semi-arid region; PRONAF Mulher is a line for financing credit proposals from female farmers; and PRONAF Jovem, which finances investments in credit proposals from young farmers and farmers. There is also rural microcredit, or PRONAF Grupo B, which aims to combat rural poverty. Microcredit is strategic for poor family farmers as it values the productive potential of this audience and allows for structuring and diversifying the productive unit. It can finance both agricultural and non-agricultural income-generating activities.

According to MDA data (2011), it serves farmer, fisher, extractive, riverine, quilombola and indigenous families who engage in productive activities in rural areas. According to MDA data (2011), from the 2002/2003 to the 2010/2011 Crop Plan, the volume of PRONAF resources offered for financing and investment rose from R$2.4 billion in the 2002/2003 Crop Plan to R$16 billion, a 572% increase. The number of contracts grew from 890,000 to over 2 million per crop year.

The Food Acquisition Program - PAA, created in 2003 as part of the Zero Hunger Program, allows for the direct acquisition of food whose prices cannot be higher or lower than regional market prices. PAA enables the formation of stocks by family agriculture organizations, allowing for marketing under more suitable market conditions. According to MDA data, between 2003 and 2009, PAA purchases totaled R$2.5 billion, benefiting 635,500 family farmer families and, on average, 7.7 million people per year through food donation.

In the field, the Brazil Without Poverty Plan aims to increase farmers' production through technical guidance and follow-up, the supply of inputs and water to the extremely poor rural population. Thus, the main actions planned for rural areas are: expanding ATER - technical assistance and rural extension services; each group of 1,000 families will have the assistance of one senior technician and ten medium-level technicians; families will have R$2,400 available for semiannual fostering during 2 years to support production and the commercialization of surplus food; access to water - providing 750,000 rural families with cisterns and simplified collective systems for human consumption, and serving 600,000 rural families with water for production; expanding the PAA (Food Acquisition Program) from 156,000 to 445,000 family farmer families by 2014 - from 66,000 extremely poor families to 255,000; expanding purchases by public and philanthropic institutions - federal hospitals, universities, prisons, and day care centers; transferring financial resources to Bolsa Família families in extreme poverty for environmental asset conservation - quarterly payment of R$300.

Another policy implemented in rural areas, starting with the Lula government, was the Territories of Citizenship Program. The Territories of Citizenship aim to overcome poverty and generate employment and income in rural areas through a sustainable territorial development strategy.

Social participation and integration of actions between the Federal Government, states, and municipalities are fundamental for building this strategy. This set of actions was carried out by the Federal Government in 120 Territories in 2010. The state of Ceará has 6 Territories of Citizenship: Cariri, Inhamuns, Central Sertão, Canindé Sertões, Sobral, Vale do Curu, and Aracati-Açu.

Another territorial development strategy, sustainable and solidary, that has also been contributing to the development of actions in the area of overcoming poverty, both in rural and urban settings, is Solidary Economy. Solidary economy actions are the result of broad consensus and convergence from the most diverse social sectors that make up the solidary economy, enterprises, support entities, universities, and public and parliamentary managers, among others.

Solidary Economy has been growing rapidly. According to SIES (Solidary Economy Information System of MTE), between 2000 and 2007, 10,145 new Solidary Economy enterprises were created, an average of 1,450 per year, suggesting that in 2010, considering only 52% of the municipalities surveyed, there were over 50,000 Solidary Economy enterprises in Brazil.

Thus, overcoming poverty in Brazil initially requires recognizing poverty as one of the expressions of the social issue, a characteristic of the structure of this society. Second, the precise identification of population segments in poverty, given the heterogeneity of situations and audiences that poverty encompasses, based on location - rural or urban - gender, age, among others.

Another relevant issue is understanding poverty as a collective problem that requires efforts from the government and society. Implementing strategies to overcome poverty involves both institutional and governance capacity, human resources, financial and physical resources, as well as availability and coordination with other public social policies, such as education, health, social assistance, social security, housing, labor, culture, among others.

Regarding society, it is necessary to recognize and support actions already developed by the entire civil society, whether from popular movements in the city and countryside, or from universities and non-governmental organizations that address poverty - actions in rural education, popular education, solidary economy, among others.

It is also necessary to strengthen the articulation between economic and social policies and reinforce the articulation between economic and social development.

With this, it is necessary to adopt strategies that combine universal and targeted policies, supported by the dimension of rights that guarantee an adequate network of services for attending the heterogeneous needs of the audience and their territories.

As Carla Bronzo (2005) states, in the field of public action, intersectorial and territorial policies are needed, a flexible and sensitive mode of service provision to the heterogeneous needs of populations and territories, with adequate service networks for attending, and substantively, in terms of content, oriented towards autonomy and empowerment of the served audience.

Finally, it is concluded by highlighting the collective effort that the government, society, and Parliament, among other subjects, must make together to achieve the political horizon of overcoming poverty, articulating economic growth with social justice. From the perspective of our societal project, this is one of the many dreams that moves us to continue fighting.

THE PRESIDENT (Marcio Macedo) – The floor is open to Deputy Assis Melo.

DEPUTY ASSIS MELO (Bloc/PCdoB-RS. The following remarks were made.) – Mr. President, I rise to the floor to honor the city of Caxias do Sul, which celebrated 121 years on June 20.

This history began before Italian immigration, when drovers passed through the area between the southern part of the state and the country’s center, and the indigenous Caingang people started to occupy the region in what was known as the Bugres Field.

During the second half of the 19th century, economic hardships in Italy spurred immigration to Brazil, beginning in 1875.

Immigrants arrived in Bugres Field starting in 1876, and after two years, the area was renamed Colonia de Caxias. The Municipality of Caxias do Sul was officially founded on June 20, 1890.

From the beginning of its history to the present day, the city has gone through various economic cycles, which has allowed for the diversification of productive activities. Among the first to stand out is grape cultivation and wine production. Grape and wine production continues to be one of the city’s main hallmarks, which also promotes tourism, with the celebration of the largest festival in the South, the Grape Festival.

These characteristics of Caxias do Sul are decisive in boosting other cities in the Gaúcha Mountain region. We can say that Caxias do Sul has developed and contributes to the development of other cities.

I extend a special greeting to the citizens of Caxias, who, with their dedication and commitment, build prosperity in our region, which has high development indices.

To conclude, Mr. President, I would also like to point out that our city today, Caxias do Sul, has a very large industrial potential and is the base of the metal-mechanical pole today. In the last period of 2010, Caxias had growth higher than many countries in the world. To give you an idea, the industry in Caxias do Sul grew by 31.8%. And speaking of growth, I cannot fail to highlight the struggle of the metalworkers in that city who are on strike for better wages.

Mr. President, I request that the remainder of my speech be recorded in the Annals and disseminated by the House’s communication organs.

Thank you.

Mr. President, ladies and gentlemen Members, interviews with the Governor of Sergipe, Marcelo Déda, were published yesterday in Valor Econômico and today in Estado, expressing his opinions on tax reform and the pre-salt.

Déda stated that tax reform cannot merely mean the unification of ICMS with the Northeast, North, and Central West states. Tax reform should ensure revenue that instruments a regional development policy, so necessary for these regions.

I believe this is a good opportunity for Parliament to reflect on a fundamental issue for the country, and that instead of dividing us, it should unite us. Fiscal warfare among states weakens federal relations and must be overcome. The Lula government reduced income inequality in Brazil, as never seen before, so we must think of a tax policy that perpetuates this achievement and does not deepen economic inequality among states. The President herself, Dilma, stated in her inauguration speech: "Only tax reform allows for sustainable expansion of industry and growth."

We need to reflect on the tax reform we want. Or better yet, if we want a real reform or just a new regulation of ICMS. A reform demands an agenda of negotiations that does not only have a technical focus, but also considers regional realities and the notion of the country's development as a whole, where it does not make sense to label winners and losers.

Similarly, Déda pondered on the issue of the pre-salt. Agreeing that producing states have a right to receive a larger share of royalties, the governor, however, defended a new distribution model, as this wealth belongs to the country and should serve it in its entirety.

I have no doubt that the President has worked to ensure that the Northeast, North, and Central West have their benefits guaranteed and continue on the path of sustainable development and regional development to definitively overcome differences between South, Southeast, Northeast, North, and Central-West Brazil.

Thank you.
