And it acts differently in cities, in the countryside, and in the various regions of the country to benefit the 16 million poorest Brazilians, wherever they may be.
In the countryside, where 47% of the plan's beneficiaries live, the priority is to increase the farmer's production through technical guidance and monitoring, the offer of inputs and water. Now let's look at some of the main strategies of Brazil Without Poverty in rural areas.
TECHNICAL ASSISTANCE
The poorest farmers will receive continuous and individualized monitoring by professional teams hired primarily in the region by the Federal Government. Each group of 1,000 families will be assisted by one senior technician and ten medium-level technicians. A partnership with universities and EMBRAPA will introduce appropriate technologies for each family and thus increase production.
PROMOTION AND SEEDS
Brazil Without Poverty will support extremely poor families in food production and the commercialization of their production. Each family will receive a non-repayable promotion of R$2,400, paid in semi-annual installments over two years, to acquire inputs and equipment. By 2014, 250,000 families will be assisted. The plan provides for other complementary actions to the promotion, such as the offer of EMBRAPA seeds and appropriate technologies for each region.
WATER FOR ALL PROGRAM
The goal here is to assist 750,000 families with the construction of cisterns and simplified collective systems. In addition, thousands of families will be benefited by water systems focused on production.
FOOD ACQUISITION PROGRAM (PAA)
The PAA is one of the most effective programs in expanding the market for small farmers. Through it, the Federal Government purchases production to donate it to welfare entities or to form stocks. With Brazil Without Poverty, the PAA will be significantly expanded. Currently, it assists 66,000 families.

**Mil Families in Extreme Poverty, Until 2014**

**Will Benefit 255,000.**

**Purchase of Production**

Another planned action is to expand public purchases for hospitals, universities, prisons, creches, and also for the private supply network, such as supermarkets and restaurants, which will begin to count on the production of the poorest farmers.

**No Poverty in Cities**

In urban areas, the central goal of Brazil Without Poverty will be to generate employment and income for the poorest, between the ages of 18 and 65, through professional qualification courses, employment mediation, expansion of microcredit policy, and encouragement of popular and solidary economy, among other social inclusion actions that should benefit 2 million people. Action lines include:

**MAP OF OPPORTUNITIES**

The Federal Government, along with states and municipalities, will identify a range of opportunities available in cities to include productively the families identified by the Poverty Map. Thus, by combining these two tools, Brazil Without Poverty will promote a more inclusive economic growth, generating new job and income opportunities.

**WORKFORCE QUALIFICATION**

The goal is to insert Bolsa Família beneficiaries into the job market through training courses aligned with the economic vocation of each region. Technical schools, the System S, and other networks will be mobilized to offer over 200 types of free and certified courses. Students will receive pedagogical material, snacks, and transportation.

**PUBLIC INTERMEDIATION OF WORKFORCE**

Intermediation actions will be carried out considering the range of opportunities mapped along with public and private companies. Beneficiaries of Bolsa Família and individuals aged 18 to 65 will be selected as priorities.

**SUPPORT FOR ORGANIZING WASTE COLLECTORS OF RECYCLABLE MATERIALS**

Brazil Without Poverty will strongly support municipalities in implementing selective collection programs. This will benefit the environment, strengthen existing catador cooperatives, and open thousands of jobs in this sector.

**PROGRAM RESULTS**

Aiming at the productive inclusion of the poorest population, Brazil Without Poverty will, among other actions, promote the articulation of various government programs. The goal is to create new opportunities for

Deputy Luciano Castro, I grant the floor to Deputy Zé Geraldo of the PT for a Leadership Statement, in accordance with Article 89 of the Internal Regulation, for 10 minutes.

MR. ZÉ GERALDO (PT-PA. As Leader. Without revision of the speaker.) – Mr. President, Ladies and Gentlemen Deputies, Ladies and Gentlemen, all those listening to me at this moment, this week I participated in two intense hearings, two intense negotiations. The first was on Monday, practically all day. It was more than 8 hours of hearing with the coordinates of the MST – Movement of Landless Workers, the FETAGRI – Federation of Workers in Agriculture, and the FETRAF – National Federation of Workers and Family Farmers in Agriculture, movements that represent the settlements of agrarian reform, the campistas from the South and Southeast regions of Pará, more precisely from Marabá.

Yesterday, there was a meeting between representatives of the Ministry of Justice, Mayors, representatives of rural workers from the region of Altamira, from the pole, from the territory of Xingu, where the Belo Monte dam will be built. In this hearing, FUNAI – National Indian Foundation, the Ministry of Justice, the Mayors and the farmers discussed the situation of over a thousand families that have been on the land for 10 or 20 years, some even longer, and who now have to be removed due to a FUNAI decree on the demarcation of the indigenous land of Cachoeira Seca.

In the municipalities of Uruará and Placas, over a thousand families are registered with INCRA to be settled, for 5 years, and so far there have been no settlements for them.

We are facing a situation, in the North Region of Brazil, particularly in the State of Pará, that deserves special attention from the Federal Government, from the Ministry of Planning, from the Ministry of Agriculture, Development and from INCRA. It is necessary to give speed to the solution of these problems. I am a bit worried about this model of settlement that has been ongoing in the Amazon since the military time. Indeed, I am a resident beneficiary of the colonization project built by President Médici. After more than 30 years, there are still many things to be resolved in it. That is why I presented two requests this week, to the Amazon Commission and to the Environment Commission. I am a member of both commissions and I am proposing the holding of a seminar at the beginning of August to debate agrarian reform, the development of family production in the Amazon Region, a continental-sized region that differs quite a bit from others.

One of the errors that have been committed over these 30 years is the settlement of families in

distant locations from cities, from highways. This distance alone makes settlements unviable. Evidence of this is that, after 10, 20 years, some settled families end up selling their property and buying a small farm, a property on the outskirts of a city, in order for their lives to improve. It seems to me that we have to start exactly from this point. Land reform can be more expensive at first, because the Government will have to buy land along the highways, but in the medium and long term, it will be cheaper and more viable, as we won't have family evictions, as in current settlements. The INCRA settled families 10, 12 years ago, and the infrastructure has still not been resolved. Governments have been working under pressure. Some families moved to those Northern states, mainly Pará; a large part went to Maranhão and Piauí; and many others sought better days in government-incented programs, in mines. Now, these families have no way back, have no other employment alternative and need to seek survival on the land. It's time to rethink land reform. For 30 years, since I arrived in the state of Pará, I have been a defender of land reform in the Amazon. The development of family farming in the Amazon will only be possible if settlements are made along the rivers or along the highways.

The state of Pará today has over 5,000 kilometers of federal highways, many already paved, others in the process of paving, such as Cuiabá-Santarém and Transamazônica. Probably, by the end of 2014, they will all be 100% paved. Just these two highways have a distance of 2,000 kilometers, and many lands along these highways could be bought by the Federal Government and designated for family settlement. Thus, of course, energy will come more easily, the doctor will come more easily, educational follow-up, school transport, production will come more easily to the cities - freight is lower, and what families need to buy also arrives at a lower price.

Today, the opposite occurs: what is produced is sold at a lower price and other products are bought at a higher price. In this exchange, there is impoverishment, dis-capitalization and bankruptcy of many families settled by INCRA.

Another point: infrastructure. It's no use implementing the "Light for All" program, a policy that deserves commendations. We need to advance in providing electric power to all communities. In the state of Pará, there are communities that have electric power, and farmers even set up a small factory there to produce cheese during the period...

Regarding the rains. But the cheese cannot be exported
because there is no road.
This is the other great challenge: increasing resources
for infrastructure in the land reform settlements of
the State of Pará.
Thank you very much.

BILL No. 1.652, of 2011
(from Mr. Laercio Oliveira)
Provides for the deduction from taxable profit, for purposes of income tax on legal entities, of twice the expenses incurred in professional training projects, and provides for other measures.

The National Congress decrees and I sanction the following Law:

Article 1. Legal entities may deduct from taxable profit, for purposes of income tax, twice the expenses duly proven to have been incurred, in the base period, in professional training projects, approved and monitored by the Ministry of Labor."

**Single Paragraph.** The deduction referred to in the heading of this article shall not exceed, for each financial year, 1% (one percent) of the taxable profit, and expenses not deducted in the corresponding financial year may be carried forward for deduction in the following three financial years, and cumulatively with the Worker Food Program – PAT, as provided in Article 1 of Law No. 6,321 of April 14, 1976, to 4% (four percent).

**Article 2.** For the purposes of this Law, vocational training shall include activities carried out on national territory by legal entities entitled to the deduction provided for in Article 1, with the aim of immediately preparing individuals, whether minors or adults, for work through methodological learning, professional qualification, and technical improvement and specialization at all levels.

**§ 1.** Expenses incurred in the construction or installation of vocational training centers, including the acquisition of equipment, as well as those for the teaching of primary school for learning and supplementary education, secondary school, and higher education, may, provided they are included in the vocational training programs of the legal entities entitled to the deduction, be considered for the purposes of deduction.

**§ 2.** Expenses incurred by legal entities entitled to the deduction with apprentices enrolled in learning courses referred to in Article 429 of the Consolidation of Labor Laws and Decree-Law No. 8,622 of January 10, 1946, may also be considered for the purposes of deduction.

**Article 3.** The exemptions from the contribution to the National Industrial Apprenticeship Service – SENAI – provided for in Article 5 of Decree-Law No. 4,048 of January 22, 1942; Article 5 of Decree-Law No. 4,936 of November 7, 1942; and Article 4 of Decree-Law No. 6,246 of February 5, 1944, as well as the exemptions from the contribution to the National Commercial Apprenticeship Service – SENAC – provided for in Article 6 of Decree-Law No. 8,621 of January 10, 1946, may not be granted cumulatively with the deduction provided for in Article 1 of this Law.

**Article 4º O** The Executive Branch shall establish the conditions to be observed by entities managing contributions of a parafiscal nature compulsorily collected, in accordance with the existing legislation, for the purposes of vocational training.

**Article 5º O** The Executive Branch shall regulate this Law within 60 (sixty) days of its publication.

**Article 6.** This Law shall enter into force upon its publication, repealing any contrary provisions.

This Law takes effect on the date of its publication.

Justification

Ceramics play an important role in the Brazilian economy, with a participation in the Gross Domestic Product (GDP) estimated at 1%, equivalent to approximately six billion dollars. The abundance of natural raw materials and the availability of energy sources allowed Brazilian industries to quickly gain international markets in various ceramic segments.

Diverse, the sector is divided into producers of red ceramics, coating materials, refractory materials, sanitary ware, electrical porcelain insulators, tableware, artistic ceramics (decorative and useful), ceramic water filters for domestic use, technical ceramics, and thermal insulators.

The Pioneering Spirit of Porto Ferreira

In the field of artistic ceramics, the municipality of Porto Ferreira stands out greatly, both for its significant production and the splendor of its products. Located in the central region of the State of São Paulo, 220 km from the capital, the municipality had its first ceramic factory, the “Porto Ferreira Pottery Factory,” founded as early as the 1920s, which gave rise to the process of industrialization of that locality, which would become a prominent national production center.

In 1931, a group of entrepreneurs, led by Djalma Forjaz, purchased the equipment of the city’s first industry and founded the “Cerâmica Porto Ferreira.” Engineer Forjaz, throughout his long career, held a prominent position in the development of the Brazilian ceramic industry.

From the first ceramic factory, many others were gradually established in Porto Ferreira. In the 1980s, the municipality had over 800 productive establishments in full operation.

The National Congress decrees:
Article 1. People affected by neuromuscular diseases with motor paralysis shall receive, primarily from the Unique Health System (SUS), the essential medications and equipment for their survival, including those necessary for associated comorbidities.
§ 1. The list of neuromuscular diseases with motor paralysis to be covered by this law shall be defined by the Executive Power in a separate act.
§ 2. The Executive Power, through the Ministry of Health, shall select the medications and equipment referred to in the preceding paragraph, with a view to guiding their acquisition by SUS managers.
§ 3. The selection referred to in § 2 shall be reviewed and republished annually or whenever necessary to adapt to current scientific knowledge and the availability of new medications, technologies, and products in the market.
Article 2. Medications and equipment necessary for patients covered by this Law may be delivered to their respective residences previously registered with the competent health authorities, without any cost to the user.
Sole Paragraph. An agreement may be established between the competent SUS authority and state or Federal District or municipal health bodies for the priority delivery of the medications and equipment referred to in the first paragraph.
Article 3. Non-profit entities that have demonstrably acted in the area and have received certification as a charitable entity of social assistance in accordance with applicable legislation may enter into an agreement with the competent SUS authority or with a state or Federal District or municipal body that is a SUS-convenied entity for the delivery of equipment and the care of people affected by neuromuscular diseases with motor paralysis.
Article 4. It is guaranteed to a person affected by a neuromuscular disease with motor paralysis the right to receive, in writing, within 48 (forty-eight) hours from the date of their request, information regarding the unavailability of medications and equipment by the same health authority.
Article 5. The Union shall promote scientific research, including that which uses gene therapy, aimed at preventing, treating, and curing neuromuscular diseases with motor paralysis.
Article 6. This Law shall enter into force on the first day of the subsequent financial year following its publication.

Justification
This project aims to provide priority treatment to individuals affected by neuromuscular diseases with motor paralysis. There are numerous diseases that fall under this category, and the established priority serves only those whose health condition poses a risk to their own survival. The focus of this proposal is, therefore, to protect life by distributing medications and equipment on a priority basis to individuals with neuromuscular diseases with motor paralysis.

Among the various forms of neuromuscular diseases with motor paralysis, there is a common denominator: respiratory distress caused by the lack of strength in the respiratory muscles.

In most neuromuscular patients, respiratory insufficiency begins with a decrease in lung volumes and progressive weakness of inspiratory and expiratory muscles, followed by pulmonary infections, respiratory disturbances during sleep, and ultimately, daytime respiratory failure. The main problem in neuromuscular diseases is hypoventilation, which leads to hypercapnia. CO2 levels and arterial blood gas analysis should be periodically evaluated, depending on clinical circumstances1.

In the treatment of respiratory weaknesses, one of the most efficient methods currently available is the use of air stacking and cough assist techniques.

However, what truly makes a difference is the application of air stacking techniques (air holding exercises with an ambu or manual resuscitator), glottic-pharyngeal breathing (GPB), also known as "frog breathing," and cough assist, which serve a dual function for patients with neuromuscular diseases as they facilitate the elimination of tracheobronchial secretions and promote lung re-expansion (air stacking with cough assist).

The BiPAP (Bilevel Positive Airway Pressure) device, which contributes to respiratory treatment, has been distributed by the SUS (National Health System) since Portaria 1.531 2001, initially restricted to patients with muscular dystrophy. In 2008, the Ministry of Health issued portaria 1.370, establishing that every patient with a neuromuscular disease has the right to receive the equipment. Despite significant progress over the past decade, the fight continues for the release of other equipment that aids in the more advanced stages of the disease, such as cough assist and volumetric ventilators.

It is important to note that the use of these devices represents an effective economy for public funds, as patients using them would otherwise require hospitalization1.

ROL DE DOENÇAS NEUROMUSCULARES
The systematic and statistical classification of neurological diseases dates back to the early 19th century. However, it was only in 1946, at the International Health Conference in New York, with the preparation of the sixth revision of the International List of Diseases and Causes of Death, that neuromuscular diseases received more detailed attention.
Among the diseases cataloged, the chapter on neuromuscular diseases (NMDs) stands out, particularly because many of them present severe and incapacitating motor impairment.
Neuromuscular diseases represent a large group of conditions that affect the motor unit, that is, the cell body of the lower motor neuron, its axon, the neuromuscular junction, or the skeletal muscle tissue.
For the classification of the numerous neuromuscular diseases, it is useful to follow the anatomical path of the lower motor neuron, thus allowing the identification and diagnosis of the main specific diseases in each primary topographic site.

**MOTOR NEURONOPATHY:**

The spectrum of diseases affecting the cell body of the motor neuron, known as motor neuronopathies, is vast and significant due to their clinical peculiarities.

Various presentation forms can be distinguished based on genetic characteristics (autosomal dominant inheritance, autosomal recessive inheritance, X-linked inheritance), the mode of onset (acute, insidious), the age of symptom onset (neonatal, childhood, adolescence, adulthood), the rate of progression (slowly progressive, clinical stabilization, rapidly progressive), and the preference for motor involvement (asymmetric, symmetric, proximal, distal, upper limbs, lower limbs, bulbar region). Associated symptoms and signs are important for clinical characterization. Electroneuromyographic study is fundamental for clinical characterization. The development of DNA testing has enabled more precise characterization of certain diseases, leading to a better understanding of pathophysiology.

Main related conditions include:

**ACUTE ANTERIOR POLYMYELITIS:** A viral disease now eradicated in our country, affecting the NMI and causing motor deficit, predominantly in the lower limbs, usually asymmetrically. Patients affected by poliomyelitis, when subjected to intense rehabilitation programs, often show significant functional improvement.

**POST-POLIOMYELITIS SYNDROME (PPS):** Characterized by the appearance of new muscle weakness years after acute infection with the poliovirus, and clinical stabilization, related to the degeneration of surviving motor units, perhaps due to "overuse" (overtraining). PPS diagnosis is made by exclusion, differentiating it from other neurological, orthopedic, or psychiatric conditions that may present a similar picture.

**SPINAL MUSULAR ATROPHY (SMA):** Refers to pure NMI diseases of genetic origin with great clinical heterogeneity. This definition implies no involvement of the CNS or sensitivity (Table 1).

The most known forms of SMA are those of
autosomal recessive inheritance, with the genetic
locus mapped on chromosome 5q 11-2-13.3 (SMA 5q),
related to the SMN protein (survival motor neuron –
neural survival gene). Basically, there are three distinct
clinical manifestation forms, depending on their severity:
TYPE I OR FATAL – Werdnig-Hoffmann disease.
Clinically, it manifests with neonatal hypotonia, intense
muscular weakness, including swallowing and breathing
musculature, with death usually before one year of age,
especially due to respiratory problems. Differential
diagnosis is made with conditions that present hypotonia
in childhood, but the severity of the picture, respiratory
musculature compromise, and innervation by bulbar
cranial nerves (bulbar musculature) and, sometimes,
tongue fasciculations allow strong clinical suspicion.
TYPE II – Intermediate. Usually manifests in the first
half of the first year of life with generalized muscular
weakness. Most children are able to move their limbs and
acquire walking. Survival until adolescence is the rule.
Prognosis depends on the degree of intercostal weakness
and respiratory deficit. Differential diagnosis with
childhood muscular dystrophies can sometimes be
difficult. An important point, however, is the pseudo-
hypertrophy, rare in SMA cases.
TYPE III – Kugelberg Welander disease. Typically,
between 5 and 15 years old, although it can start earlier
and has a more favorable course. In some patients, certain
motor improvement is observed, presumably as a result
of compensatory reinervation of the muscle. On the other
hand, some patients present unexpected motor deterioration,
often between 8 and 10 years of age, with loss of
walking, which is also not uncommon after an incidental
problem such as trauma, fracture, or even surgery.
More recently, other forms of SMA have been reported,
deserving attention:
TYPE IV or ADULT SMA: genetically more
heterogeneous, with forms of autosomal recessive,
autosomal dominant, and X-linked recessive inheritance
described. Most patients develop clinical manifestations
around the age of 30, with muscular weakness predominating
in the proximal portions of the lower limbs, in a
symmetrical form. Tongue fasciculations and hand
tremor are rarely seen.

**Distal Autosomal Recessive (Chromosome 11), with Mutation in the IGHMBP2 Gene, Causing Distal Muscle Weakness, Early, Associated with Diaphragmatic Muscle Weakness, Leading to Death Before 6 Months of Life.**

**DISTAL MUSCLE WEAKNESS: The group of patients presenting with symmetric and distal muscle weakness in both upper and lower extremities is genetically heterogeneous. There are descriptions of both autosomal dominant and autosomal recessive forms. Clinical progression varies. The main differential diagnosis to be considered is Hereditary Motor Neuropathy (Charcot-Marie-Tooth Type 2 - CMT 2). In CMT 2, muscle weakness, ataxia, and tremor are more prominent, and sensory action potentials are abnormal or absent.

**MONOMELIC AMYOTROPHY OF MEMBERS:**
 Represents a heterogeneous disorder characterized by neurogenic atrophy in one limb, either upper or lower. It most frequently affects males, with initial symptoms in the second or third decades, progressing slowly. There is no associated impairment of the NMS, sensitivity, cerebellum, or extrapyramidal systems. Hirayama was the first to describe the clinical presentation of muscle atrophy and weakness in the hands and forearms, proposing the term Unilateral Upper Extremity Muscular Atrophy. Later, finding association with contralateral involvement in 1/3 of patients, he changed the term to Unilateral Distal Spinal Muscular Atrophy. Although distal muscle weakness predominates, proximal muscles, such as biceps and triceps, can also be affected.

Many patients with unilateral restricted muscular atrophy in the lower limbs have been described in India, with only a few cases reported in the West. Most individuals described are male. Muscle atrophy is more evident, with little incapacitating motor impairment.

**MUSCLE WEAKNESS WITH MUTATION IN THE VAPB GENE:**
 Described in Brazil (Nishimura et al, 2004), it is clinically characterized by symptom onset between 25-40 years of age, with variable progression. Symptoms and signs of NMI impairment predominate, particularly in proximal portions of the limbs, and tremor and respiratory failure may be associated. Some patients present signs of NMS impairment, justifying the original description as a variant of ALS (ALS type 8). Mutation in the Vesicle-Associated Membrane Protein-Associated Protein B (VAPB) gene has been implicated as the causal factor. Vesicles associated with membrane proteins form intracelular complexes that promote the fusion and transport of cytoplasmic vesicles.

**FAZIO-LONDE SYNDROME (Progressive Bulbar Paralysis in Children):**
A rare form of AME characterized by decreased number of cranial motor neurons with subsequent loss.

Motor neuron disease (MND) is a generic term, frequently used to include clinical syndromes, depending on the primary site of motor neuron involvement, morphological alterations, pattern of inheritance, electrophysiological findings, and biochemical and immunological abnormalities. Included in this group are Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS), primary lateral sclerosis, progressive bulbar palsy, and progressive muscular atrophy.

Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS): Characterized by marked progressive paralysis with signs of involvement of the motor neuron system (clonus and Babinski sign) and lower motor neuron system (atrophy and fasciculations). It is the most common form of motor neuron disease and the term ALS is often used indistinctly for the other forms of MND. Clinically, it affects males more frequently than females (2:1), more whites than blacks, occurs in the sixth or seventh decades, with a progressive, incurable course, and death occurs around 36 months after the onset of initial symptoms, usually due to respiratory failure. Rare cases have survived more than ten years, and others have died in less than one year. About 5-10% of all ALS cases are represented by a familial form, with autosomal dominant inheritance being the most common.

Progressive Bulbar Palsy (PBP): Characterized by predominant involvement of bulbar muscle innervation, with or without involvement of the motor neuron system. Dysarthria and dysphagia are predominant symptoms, followed by weakness, atrophy, and fasciculations of the tongue. Moderate involvement of neck muscles may be present. Signs of motor neuron system involvement and emotional lability may be present.

Primary Lateral Sclerosis (PLS): Characterized by an insidious, slow-evolving course, without signs and symptoms of involvement of any other part of the nervous system, except the corticobulbar and corticospinal tracts.

Progressive Muscular Atrophy (PMA): A pure disease of the lower motor neuron system, of unknown cause; it is rare, accounting for about 5-20% of MND cases. Clinically, it manifests with weakness, atrophy, and fasciculations, usually beginning in the upper limbs, progressively involving the lower limbs and bulbar region. Deep reflexes are abolished. The progression of the disease may be rapid, as in ALS, or slower, with periods of clinical stabilization.

Other diseases that involve the lower motor neuron system and deserve mention are:

Kennedy's Disease: Also known as X-linked bulbar spinal atrophy, presents a mutation in the gene encoding the androgen receptor.

These may be confused with motor neuronopathies.

PARANEOPLASMIC NEUROPATIES: refers to a group
of disorders characterized clinically by rapidly progressive
motor neuropathy, with asymmetric weakness of
predominantly the lower limbs, related to a tumor. The
main descriptions, though rare, are associated with lymphomas,
such as Hodgkin's disease, which presents an aggressive course
with predominance in the lower extremities during the
remission or irradiation phase. On the other hand, we
can have a slowly progressive course with remission
after several months, demonstrating degeneration of
the anterior horn cells of the spinal cord and some
sensory tracts. Involvement of the lower motor neuron
has been associated with paraneoplastic syndromes

LOWER MOTOR NEURON SYNDROME FROM RADIATION:
This is a rare late complication of radiation to the spinal cord, particularly in the paraaortic region from malignant testicular tumors or lymphoma. It appears approximately months to years after radiation, with flaccid paraparesis, usually asymmetric, accompanied by areflexia and fasciculations. Magnetic resonance imaging of the spine does not show spinal cord abnormalities.
HEXOSAMINIDASE A AND B DEFICIENCY:
Deficiency of beta hexosaminidase A and B, also known as Tay-Sachs and Sandhoff disease, is a severe degenerative disorder caused by the accumulation, in the lysosomes of neurons, of the ganglioside GM2, which is degraded by this enzyme. It presents in three forms (infantile, juvenile, and adult), with variable onset of clinical manifestations and severity, which depends on residual activity in each individual for ganglioside degradation. The clinical course varies among family members and includes spinocerebellar degeneration, motor neuron disease, and pure cerebellar syndromes. At least one mutation in each of the three recessive genes, HexA, HexB, and GM2, which code for the enzymatic units that catalyze degradation of ganglioside GM2, is present. Adult patients with hexosaminidase A (Hex A) deficiency may exhibit clinical manifestations similar to amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). Hex A gene mutations are common in the Ashkenazi Jewish population.

BRACHIAL PLEXUS INJURIES USUALLY ARE SUBDIVIDED ACCORDING TO THE TOPOGRAPHIC SITE OF INJURY, INTO PROXIMAL OR DISTAL, WITH THE CLAVICLE AS A CRITICAL ANATOMICAL BORDER. BRACHIAL PLEXUS INJURIES ABOVE THE CLAVICLE ARE GENERALLY SUBDIVIDED INTO PRE-GANGLIONIC (SUPERGANGLIONIC, INTRADURAL) AND POST-GANGLIONIC (INFRAGANGLIONIC, EXTRADURAL, EXTRAFORAMINAL). PROXIMAL INJURIES ARE FURTHER SUBDIVIDED INTO "UPPER PLEXUS" (INJURY TO VENTAL BRANCHES OF C5 AND C6) AND "LOWER PLEXUS" (INJURY TO VENTAL BRANCHES OF C8 AND T1); C7 REPRESENTS THE "WATER DIVIDER" BETWEEN THE TWO TYPES OF PARALYSIS AND IS USUALLY UNAFFECTED IN EITHER INJURY. INJURIES CAN BE PARTIAL (INCOMPLETE) OR TOTAL (COMPLETE).

The distinction is important, as most lesions with unfavorable evolution occur in complete lesions and persist for more than 2 to 3 months.

Since the upper extremity receives its motor and sensory pathways entirely from the brachial plexus, lesions of the brachial plexus can present with a wide variety of clinical manifestations, depending on the portion of its involvement. In brachial plexus paralysis, the ventral branches of several spinal nerves that supply the plexuses are damaged. They contain both motor and sensory fibers, resulting in a combination of motor and sensory disorders. The resulting paralysis is always flaccid. In complete brachial plexus injury, there is no involvement of the rhomboid and anterior serratus muscles, as they are innervated by nerves emerging directly from roots proximal to the plexus.

LUMBAR PLEXUS INJURIES: The lumbar plexus is situated protected in the depth of the pelve and, therefore, its injury is less common than that of the brachial plexus, which is more superficial (more exposed to injuries). Most lumbar plexus injuries are related to compromise within the basin, which protects the lumbar plexus from direct traumas, being affected in conditions of great severity. The clinical diagnosis of lumbar plexus injury depends on the demonstration of a defined pattern of muscular weakness, sensory alteration, and reflex alteration that cannot be explained by a restriction to a nerve root or peripheral nerve lesion. Not surprisingly, many plexus injuries are anatomically restricted in their early stages, making their precise topographic diagnosis difficult. Nevertheless, the plexus often presents with a combination of motor, sensory, and autonomic symptoms.

**Neuropathies**

Neuropathies can be classified according to the predominant involvement, axonal or demyelinizing, as well as according to the clinical onset form, acute, subacute, or chronic. If only one nerve is involved, it is characterized as mononeuropathy. Involvement of several nerves in an asymmetric and temporal manner refers to multiple mononeuropathy. The term peripheral polyneuropathy is reserved for the involvement of several nerves in a symmetric and simultaneous manner. Clinical manifestations can be motor, sensory, or autonomic, with distal predominant symptomatology. Sensory abnormalities can be characterized by dysesthesia, hyperesthesia, or hypesthesia. Parestesia refers to the complaint of sensory alteration. Disestesia is a change in the perception of a stimulus, i.e., a tactile stimulus causing painful sensation. Hyperestesia refers to increased sensitivity to a stimulus, usually of an unpleasant quality. Hypesthesia is a decrease in sensitivity to touch or painful stimuli.

**Multiple Mononeuropathy**

Main causes include leprosy, vasculitis, diabetes, and sarcoidosis.

**Peripheral Polyneuropathy**

- **Acute Axonal**

The main example is acute intermittent porphyria, an autosomal dominant disorder resulting from the deficient activity of the heme group's hydroxymethylbilane enzyme in hemoglobin. It is one of the rare neuropathies where motor deficit may predominate in the proximal portions of the limbs. Abdominal pain and autonomic impairment are associated.

- **Subacute Axonal**

Notable causes include toxic and pharmacological agents, malnutrition, uremia, diabetes, rheumatic diseases (Systemic Lupus Erythematosus, Rheumatoid Arthritis), hypothyroidism, AIDS, sarcoidosis, and paraneoplastic syndromes.

– AXONAL CRÔNICA
Notable causes include diabetes, malnutrition, uremia, paraproteinemia, and Hereditary Sensory and Motor Neuropathy Type II.

– UNIFORM DEMYELINATING
Major representatives include Hereditary Sensory and Motor Neuropathy Type I (Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease) and Type III (Dejerine-Sottas disease), Refsum disease, Krabbe disease, and metacromic leukodystrophy.

– ACUTE NON-UNIFORM DEMYELINATING
Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS). GBS is of vital importance in the chapter of neuromuscular diseases due to its clinical peculiarities, the possibility of reversibility and complete recovery, and primarily the care required in an Intensive Care Unit. Clinically, it manifests as a symmetrical motor deficit, acute onset, generally following an infectious event (IVAS, GECA) or even vaccination, with progressive and ascending character and with areflexia. Cranial nerve involvement is often associated, particularly the facial nerve. Approximately 20% of cases require ICU treatment due to respiratory compromise. The prognosis is generally good, with complete reversibility of neurological impairment in about 60% of affected individuals, but motor sequelae are not infrequent, occasionally leading to physical disability.

– CHRONIC NON-UNIFORM DEMYELINATING
The main representative is Chronic Inflammatory Demyelinating Polyradiculoneuropathy, which differs from GBS by presenting a more insidious onset and a more progressive course. Frequently, muscle weakness reaches its peak after 2 months of symptom onset, with a progressive or relapsing-remitting course. It is an autoimmune disease with the formation of anti-myelin antibodies. It can progress with progressive worsening, potentially causing physical incapacitation, even with treatment with corticosteroids, immunosuppressants, plasmapheresis, or immunoglobulin.

– CHRONIC UNIFORM DEMYELINATING
Major representatives are Hereditary Sensory and Motor Neuropathy Types I (Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease) and III (Dejerine-Sottas disease). Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease is the most common form of hereditary neuropathy in adults, clinically characterized by the typical atrophy of the lower limbs, resembling the "swan-like" legs.

POLYNEUROPATHY: metabolic (diabetes, hypothyroidism, amyloidosis, Fabry disease), uremia, deficiency (beriberi, pellagra), toxic (alcohol, organophosphate), drug-induced (isoniazid, chloramphenicol, flagyl, vincristine), infectious (HIV, tuberculosis), inflammatory (Guillain-Barré syndrome), tumoral (myeloma, lymphoma).

GENETIC CAUSED NEUROPATHIES
PORPHYRIC NEUROPATHY: is, most often, an acute peripheral neuropathy of motor predominance, commonly associated with porphyrin crisis exacerbation, characterized by abdominal pain, vomiting, tachycardia, as well as confusional and convulsive states. The acute episode is almost always precipitated by drugs, particularly barbiturates, contraceptive pills, and alcohol. The neuropathy initially affects the upper extremities, with the lower extremities less affected. There is a long list of triggers for crises, with alcohol, sulfa, and phenytoin standing out.

FAMILIAL AMYLOIDOSIS: The most important of familial amyloidoses is the Portuguese type or Corino de Andrade disease, which presents with autosomal dominant inheritance. The disease begins insidiously between 25 and 35 years of age, with hyperesthesia and dysesthesias in the lower extremities. Plantar fasciitis then develops, followed by difficulty in walking. The autonomic nervous system is severely affected. This is one of the disease's characteristics, leading to sexual impotence, postural hypotension, and diarrhea. Superficial sensitivity is significantly impaired compared to deep sensitivity, which remains almost normal. Progression is gradual and fatal after 10 to 20 years from the onset. Diagnosis is made by demonstrating the presence of amyloid in various tissues, such as rectal mucosa, skin, and peripheral nerves. Amyloid fibers are derived predominantly from mutant forms of plasma protein, transtiretin (TTR), with valine replaced by methionine at position 30. There is no specific medication proven to be effective for the disease. Liver transplantation stabilizes the clinical picture.

HEREDITARY SENSITIVO-MOTOR NEUROPATHIES (CHARCOT-MARIE-TOOTH)
Peroneal muscular atrophy and variants (Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease - CMT) is a heterogeneous group of hereditary peripheral neuropathies, generally with autosomal dominant inheritance, characterized by slowly progressive impairment. Symptoms begin in childhood or adolescence. The intrinsic muscles of the feet and the peroneal muscles are the first to weaken, leading legs to appear like inverted champagne bottles. As the disease progresses, atrophy of intrinsic hand muscles develops, and the muscles below the knees in the lower extremities almost disappear. Tendinous reflexes are diminished or absent, particularly in the lower extremities. Sensory impairment is very subtle, and autonomic nervous system involvement is rare. Diagnosis is based on clinical picture, electrical conduction analysis, and genetic testing.

In criteria histopathological, CMT is subdivided into
two types:
– CMT 1, characterized by nerve conduction velocity
less than 38 m/s and demyelinating hypertrrophic
neuropathy;
– CMT 2 is characterized by normal or slightly de-
creased conduction velocity, associated with axonopathy.
Many genetic loci have been associated with the
CMT1 phenotype. CMT1A, the most frequent form, is
related to a 1.5-megabase duplication on chromosome
17p11.2-12, responsible for the expression of the PMP22
(peripheral myelin protein 22) gene. CMT 1B has been
mapped to chromosome 1q21-23, related to protein P0.
CMTX1, showing recessive X-linked inheritance, is
associated with mutations encoding the gene for con-
nexin 32.
AUTONOMIC NEUROPATHIES – SENSITIVITY
They are rare and present predominantly as painless
plantar fasciculations. Since the picture is initially
only sensory, without trophic changes, it is sometimes
difficult to characterize the organicity of manifestations,
especially because electromyography may be normal.
There are two described types: type 1 of autosomal
dominant inheritance and type 2 of autosomal recessive
inheritance. Tendinous reflexes are diminished or absent,
muscle strength and muscle trophism are preserved.
There is no specific medication.
ACQUIRED NEUROPATHIES
In our environment, the most common cause of
peripheral neuropathy is leprosy, followed by al-
coholism and diabetes.
It is also important to note that about 40% of chronic
peripheral neuropathies that occur after the fifth de-
cade of life remain undiagnosed.
LEPROSY: the neurological picture of leprosy varies
according to its polarity.
TUBERCULOUS FORM: the neurological picture
presents as mononeuropathy or multiple mononeu-
ropathy, with the most affected nerves being the ulnar,
radial, peroneal, median, and retroauricular. The pal-
pable nerve is thickened and very painful. The picture
begins with pain, hypoesthesia, and paresthesias in
the territory of the affected nerve, evolving to muscle
weakness, atrophy, and finally, irreversible destruction
of the affected axons. It is essential to make the diag-
nosis in the early stages of mononeuropathy or multiple
mononeuropathy to preserve nerve integrity, even if
there is no skin lesion yet that indicates the diagnosis
of leprosy.
DIARY OF THE HOUSE OF DEPUTIES

**VIRCHOWIAN FORM: **Nerve commitment presents as distal and symmetric sensory polyneuropathy. The coldest regions of the body (ears, dorsal surfaces of hands and feet, medial dorsal surfaces of forearms, and anterolateral surfaces of thighs) are initially affected, and in the final stages, thermal-pain sensitivity is absent throughout most of the body, except for the skin covering the spine.

**DIMORPHIC AND INDETERMINATE FORMS: **The clinical picture can present in a wide range of manifestations, from those similar to the tuberculoid pole to cases resembling the Virchowian pole.

**DIABETIC NEUROPATHY: **Diabetic neuropathy develops in approximately 50% of patients with diabetes, especially those with a long history and uncontrolled glycemia (greater than 180 mg/dL). It is important to note that neuropathy can occur even in individuals with glucose intolerance. Neuropathy can manifest in various forms: sensory and/or motor and/or autonomic polyneuropathy, mononeuropathy (especially of cranial nerves), and multiple mononeuropathy. The most common form is distal and symmetric sensory polyneuropathy, which usually accompanies declared diabetes but can also appear as the first sign of the disease. Muscle weakness is not common. Distal superficial sensitivity is impaired, but pain, paresthesias, and a burning sensation in the feet are the main complaints. More severe cases also show impairment of deep and plantar sensory function. Isolated autonomic neuropathy is rare and is often associated with the described cases, manifesting primarily as sexual impotence. Other vegetative disturbances, such as sphincter impairment, postural hypotension, and diarrhea, are not frequent. Purely motor diabetic polyneuropathy is rarer.

**ALCOHOLISM: **This is a distal and symmetric sensory-motor polyneuropathy of insidious onset that occurs in alcoholic patients and affects the lower extremities more than the upper. The sensory picture, in addition to showing impairment of superficial (more intense) and deep sensitivity, also presents pain and paresthesias that predominate in the lower extremities.

**PARANEOPLASMIC: **Various types of malignant neoplasms can produce polyneuropathies by remote effect. Lung, breast, ovarian carcinomas, myelomas, lymphomas, and lymphosarcomas are the types most frequently associated with peripheral neuropathies. It is important to note that lymphomas and lymphosarcomas often affect the peripheral nervous system by direct infiltration.

Nervous, being then a metastatic process and not
paraneoplastic. There are two main types of paraneoplastic
peripheral neuropathies, sensory neuropathy and sensory-
motor neuropathy. Sensory neuropathy is characterized
by intense impairment of deep sensitivity, leading to
sensory ataxia and pseudo-athetotic movements of the
hands. It usually precedes the diagnosis of the neoplasm
by several months to several years. Onset is often subacute,
with complete loss of kinesthetic-positional and tactile
sensitivity in all four limbs, both proximal and distal.
The upper limbs are more affected than the lower ones,
and discrete impairment of superficial sensitivity in
boot and glove may be found. Tendinous reflexes are
absent. Weakness and muscle atrophy occur in the
late stages of the disease. This sensory neuropathy may
also exist unassociated with neoplasms, with the etiology
to be determined. Sensory-motor neuropathy is the
most common and manifests insidiously, usually after
the neoplasm has been detected. The clinical picture
shows more intense involvement of the lower limbs
than the upper ones, with discrete distal muscle weakness,
hyporreflexia, and impairment of sensitivity in boot
and glove.
ASSOCIATED WITH COLAGEN DISEASES AND VASCULITIS:
Collagen diseases and vasculitides can produce various
types of peripheral neuropathies, with multiple mononeuropathy
being the most common. Among the collagenopathies,
those most frequently associated with peripheral
neuropathies are periarterite nodosa (PAN) and rheumatoid
arthritis (RA), although systemic lupus erythematosus,
scleroderma, giant cell arteritis, Wegener's granulomatosis,
and others can also produce them. PAN typically produces
multiple mononeuropathy that begins with pain and
disesthesias in the region of the affected nerves, evolving
in hours or days to muscle weakness and loss of sensitivity
in the same territories. Other collagenopathies can also
produce multiple mononeuropathies, with scleroderma
more frequently producing distal sensory-motor poly-
neuropathy, and RA may produce any type of peripheral
neuropathy. Treatment consists of controlling the underlying
disease, with the use of corticosteroids and/or immunosuppressant
drugs (cyclophosphamide).
DRUG-INDUCED: Numerous medications can cause
peripheral neuropathies of various types. We will mention
some of the most important ones.

MUSCLE JOINT DISEASES

Among the diseases affecting the neuromuscular junction, the following should be highlighted:

EATON-LAMBERT SYNDROME (myastenia): it is a rare, special form, associated in 50% of cases with small cell lung cancer. The primary defect is in the presynaptic neuron, with a reduction in the number of "quanta" of acetylcholine released by the nerve impulse, caused by the presence of anti-calcium channel antibodies in the nerve terminals. In the Eaton-Lambert syndrome (unlike myasthenia), weakness is greater in the shoulder and pelvic belts and in the trunk, and involvement of muscles innervated by cranial nerves is rarer. Weakness appears with exercise, but sometimes the first movements trigger a temporary increase in muscle strength. Tendinous reflexes are hypoactive or abolished. Electromyography is very important for diagnosis and differential diagnosis with severe myasthenia. Characteristically, there is an increase in the amplitude of the muscular action potential, followed by maximal voluntary contraction. Some patients improve with the use of anticolinesterase drugs, while others only benefit from the use of guanidine 125 mg VO three to six times a day.

BOTULISM: it is a consequence of a neurotoxin produced by Clostridium botulinum, a gram-positive anaerobic bacterium that can contaminate food. Botulinum toxin is a powerful presynaptic blocker of acetylcholine release. The clinical syndrome is characterized by progressive muscle weakness, usually starting in the extraocular and pharyngeal muscles and then generalizing. Antitoxin therapy (trivalent - A, B, E) should be initiated as soon as possible. Maintaining respiratory function is the most important aspect of treatment in severe cases of botulism.

SEVERE ACQUISITIVE MYASTHENIA (SAMA): SAMA is characterized by abnormal fatigue after repetitive or sustained muscular activity and by improvement after rest. The peak incidence occurs in young adults, affecting females more frequently. Symptoms usually begin in the extrinsic ocular muscles, in the bulbar innervation region, or in the muscles of the limbs and trunk. In about 50% of patients, the eyes are initially involved, either through palpebral ptosis, usually asymmetric, or through diplopia.

Diplopia resulting from paresis of extrinsic ocular muscle. Characteristically, involvement of this muscle may alternate from one side to another on successive examinations. Bulbar muscle involvement is characterized by difficulty chewing, swallowing, and speaking. Respiratory muscles are frequently involved, particularly when the disease is advanced. Myasthenia symptoms are minimized with the use of acetylcholinesterase inhibitors (Prostigmine® or Mestinon®). Due to its autoimmune nature, with the formation of anti-acetylcholine receptor antibodies in the muscular membrane, the use of corticosteroids or other immunosuppressant drugs is part of the therapeutic arsenal. Thymectomy, not yet universally accepted, is usually reserved for cases with generalized involvement, particularly in young patients with recent onset or in those with confirmed thymoma by neuroimaging studies. Complications include limitation in performing activities of daily living, myasthenic crises (episodes of respiratory insufficiency, requiring intensive care unit admission and respiratory support).

E. MYOPATHIES
Myopathies present, most often, with proximal muscle weakness, with a change in gait pattern (pelvic tilt), falls to the ground, and difficulty rising ("pathetic rise").

- MUSCULAR DYSTROPHY
The term muscular dystrophy is reserved for primary muscular diseases of well-defined genetic inheritance, of evolutionary and incurable character.

- DUCHENNE (DMD) AND BECKER (DMB) MUSCULAR DYSTROPHY
These are the most common forms of muscular dystrophy, occurring in 1 case per 3,500 male newborns, with 2/3 of affected children having mothers who are carriers of the gene leading to disease manifestation. They are recessive X-linked allelic diseases, with the affected gene located on the short arm of chromosome X (Xp21). This gene is responsible for the synthesis of a membrane protein called dystrophin, which is absent in DMD and present but in smaller quantities than normal in DMB. In DMD, the first symptoms are detected during the onset of walking, which attracts parents' attention due to frequent falls and difficulty rising. The constant progression of the disease leads the child to be confined to a wheelchair by around age 12. Death occurs as a consequence of the disease.

used to include patients with muscle weakness distributed

6.4 – CONGENITAL MUSCULAR DYSTROPHY (CMD)
A recessive autosomal inheritance disease, characterized clinically by the presence of neonatal hypotonia, motor development delay, associated with progressive joint contractures. The clinical picture tends to stabilize, but some patients experience slow and progressive worsening. Respiratory and swallowing complications may occur. Muscle biopsy reveals the presence of atrophic, rounded fibers surrounded by connective tissue, many with significant alterations in their internal architecture. As they constitute the main limiting factor in most cases, contractures should be treated through passive physical therapy, the use of splints, or corrective surgeries.

FACIO-SCAPULO-UMERAL DYSTROPHY (FSUD)
Facio-scapulo-umeral dystrophy is the third most common form of hereditary muscle disease, affecting approximately 1 in 20,000 people. It is a dominant autosomal myopathy.

can be detected in early adolescence. In the classic form,
weakness begins simultaneously in the face and scapula,
with the peri-scapular muscles and brachial biceps most
intensely affected. Facial muscle weakness begins insidiously,
with difficulty in whistling and sucking, before eye orbicular
weakness. Pelvic floor weakness occurs late, but foot dorsiflexor
muscles are compromised early, leading to characteristic
gait, of the myopathic and scrapy type. There is no pseudo-
hypertrophy, and weakness of the peri-scapular muscles
leads to bilateral winged scapula. Progression is quite slow,
with near-normal life expectancy. Clinical diagnosis is based
on the pattern of muscle involvement, and definitive diagnosis
is made with DNA analysis (deletion in 4q35), a genetic test
with approximately 98% sensitivity.
EMERY-DREIFUSS MUSCULAR DYSTROPHY
EDM has two distinct genetic forms: X-linked (Xq28 with
alteration in the emerin protein) or autosomal dominant.

Dominant oto-facial muscular dystrophy – HAD – (1q21.2-q21.3 with alteration in laminin A/C gene).. The relationship between the protein defect and phenotype is still unclear. Clinically, it presents with the triad of early-onset contractures, slowly progressive muscle weakness, and cardiac conduction defects and/or arrhythmias. The age of clinical onset, severity, and progression of muscle and cardiac involvement show great inter- and intrafamilial variability. Generally, muscle contractures install in the first two decades, followed by muscle atrophy and weakness. Cardiac involvement often begins after the second decade of life, with no direct correlation between motor and cardiac compromise. Sudden death may be the first manifestation of the disease, especially in the HAD form. Diagnosis is made clinically and by muscle biopsy, and mainly by molecular analysis. The diagnosis of X-linked DMED is performed by immunodetection of emerin (absent in 95% of patients) and molecular testing of the DMED gene. Diagnosis of HAD-related DMED is based on laminin genetic testing. Considering that the main limiting factor for patients with DMED is cardiac compromise, with conduction block, leading to syncope and even sudden death, close cardiovascular monitoring is essential. Pacemaker and cardiac defibrillator implantation is recommended in high-risk situations. For carriers of the X-linked DMED form, often asymptomatic, close cardiovascular monitoring is advised due to the risk of developing cardiac compromise.

OCULOFARINGEAL MUSCULAR DYSTROPHY (OFMD)
Oculofaringeal muscular dystrophy is an autosomal dominant disease characterized by the presence of dysphagia, which begins in the fifth decade of life. Bilateral ptosis and significant muscle involvement innervated by the trigeminal and bulbar nerve pairs are present. Dysphagia is prominent, especially for liquids, and in the final stages of the disease, feeding and hydration can only be achieved through a gastric tube. As the disease progresses, there is muscle involvement in the trunk. The disease has been mapped to chromosome 14q11.2, with variable expansion of (GCN) trinucleotide repeats coding for alanine in the first exon of PABPN1 (nuclear polyadenylation binding protein 1). Speech therapy should be initiated as early and consistently as possible. Nasal escape during speech improves with palatine elevators.

(palatal lift). Dietary guidelines are fundamental,
aiming to avoid microaspirations and bronchopneumonia.
Surgical correction of ptosis palpebral should only be
performed when there is functional impairment of vision,
due to the numerous complications that may occur,
especially corneal ulcer. Surgery is contraindicated in
individuals with severe ophthalmoplegia, dry eye syndrome,
or weak orbicular muscle function.

– MYOTONIC SYNDROMES
The common characteristic of all myotonias is the
difficulty in relaxing the skeletal muscle after a state of
muscle contraction.

– CONGENITAL MYOTONIA (THOMSEN DISEASE)
This is a disease generally inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern, characterized by the presence of myotonia,
especially in the hands, and muscle hypertrophy, frequently.
Myotonia limits physical activity although it does not
establish true paresis.

– MYOTONIC DISTROPHY (STEINERT DISEASE)
This condition, inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern,
is the most common form of adult muscular dystrophy,
with a prevalence of 5 per 100,000. It is characterized by
the presence of myotonia, associated with paresis,
especially in distal musculature, atrophy of temporal,
masseterian, and sternocleidomastoid muscles, as well as
baldness, cataract, cardiac block, gonadal atrophy, and
low intelligence. The basic molecular abnormality consists
of an unstable DNA expansion with repeat contractions,
associated with the gene for a protein kinase. The greater
the repeat contractions, the more exuberant the disease
manifestation. It can present from birth, being more severe
in these situations.

– CONGENITAL MYOPATHIES
Under the denomination of congenital myopathies
fall several primary muscular diseases that share in common
neonatal hypotonia, delay in motor development, but with
non-progressive impairment, allowing even improvement
in motor function over time.

Diagnosis can only be made after muscle biopsy.
Depending on the specific alterations found in the biopsy,
we can distinguish Central Core Myopathy, Nemalinic,
Central Nuclear, and Congenital Fiber Disproportion,
which are the main representatives.

Central Core Myopathy assumes great importance
in this chapter due to its association with malignant
hyperthermia. Therefore, it is recommended for all cases
of neonatal hypotonia to be under careful care.

**Anesthetic Procedures, Especially Using Succinylcholine and Halothane.**

**METABOLIC MYOPATHIES**
Any alteration in energy supply to skeletal muscle causes motor function damage. The term glycogenosis is reserved for alterations in glucose metabolism, resulting in glycogen accumulation in muscle fibers; lipidosis for triglyceride accumulation; and mitochondrial pathology when mitochondrial function is affected. Diagnosis is confirmed through muscle biopsy demonstrating substrate accumulation or by identifying mitochondrial abnormalities.

**GLYCOGENOSIS**
To date, there are 9 enzymatic defects affecting skeletal muscle tissue, either alone or in association with other tissues12. The clinical presentation of different glycogenoses can range from hypotonia or muscle weakness (Type II or Pompe disease; Type III or Forbes-Cori disease) to exercise intolerance, cramps, fatigue, and myoglobinuria (Type V or McArdle disease; Type VII or Tarui disease). Pompe disease also manifests with cardiomegaly and hepatomegaly, leading to a poorer prognosis.

**McARDLE DISEASE**
This disease is related to a deficiency in myophosphorylase enzyme, responsible for breaking down the bonds between glucose molecules in glycogen. A defect in this enzyme prevents patients from using glycogen as an energy source during intense exercise. Clinically, it is characterized by exercise intolerance and pain, particularly in muscles most used for a specific function, often leading to a state of sustained muscle contraction without electrical activity (contracture). Contracture and pain indicate muscle damage, and frank myoglobinuria may occasionally occur. Patients are advised to avoid exercises that require significant glycogen supply. Symptomatology can be minimized with the use of fructose, honey, sublingual isoprenaline, or coenzyme Q10.

**LIPIDOSIS**
Lipid metabolism, also complex, is fundamental for maintaining physical activity. Carnitine, an enzyme present in the inner membrane of mitochondria, transporting long-chain fatty acids into the mitochondria, plays a significant role in this metabolism. Deficiency, caused by reduced synthesis, abnormal degradation, or inadequate transport, leads to generalized muscle weakness.

Treatment requires the oral or intravenous replacement of carnitine.

- MITOCHONDRIAL DISORDERS

Mitocondrial abnormalities are a characteristic of a wide variety of clinical syndromes, usually involving preferentially skeletal and brain muscle tissue. Clinically, they are heterogeneous diseases manifesting in many different forms: exercise intolerance; cramping; proximal muscle paresis; progressive external ocular muscle paralysis; multisystemic manifestations (Kearns Sayre Syndrome - progressive external ophtalmoplegia, pigmentary retinopathy, cardiac block, and cytological dissociation in cerebrospinal fluid; MERRF - myoclonic epilepsy with ragged-red fiber; MELAS - mitochondrial encephalopathy, lactic acidosis, and stroke-like episodes). Diagnosis is made through muscle biopsy revealing "ragged-red fiber" characterized by red staining in the sub-sarcolemmal region of muscle fibers when stained with Gomori trichrome.

NEURONAL EXCITABILITY DISORDERS

Muscle pain, stiffness, and cramping are frequently seen in neuromuscular diseases. The differential diagnosis of these symptoms is broad and includes systemic diseases, neurological disorders involving the pyramidal, extrapyramidal, and neuromuscular systems (TABLE 1). Neuromuscular diseases manifesting with muscle stiffness, cramping, and pain as predominant symptoms are referred to as "neuromuscular excitability syndrome". They include diseases affecting the central nervous system (e.g., Stiff Person Syndrome), nerves (e.g., neuromiotonia - Isaacs syndrome and its variant Morvan syndrome), and skeletal muscle (e.g., cramp/fasciculation syndrome, channelopathies, metabolic myopathies).

This group of diseases is characterized by episodes of flaccid paralysis, with a tendency to remit within hours. Different types have been described and classification depends on the serum potassium value.

Hypokalemic periodic paralyses can be primary or secondary. The primary form is inherited as an autosomal dominant trait and episodes usually begin in the second decade of life. They occur particularly in the morning, with the main triggers being increased carbohydrate intake and intense physical exercise hours beforehand. Weakness is generalized, often sparing the respiratory muscles, and can last for hours or even 2 or 3 days. Treatment is done through replacement of KCl, by oral (preferable) or intravenous route.

Hyperkalemic periodic paralyses can also be primary or secondary. In the primary form, inherited as an autosomal dominant trait, episodes are generally triggered by cold or prolonged fasting and last from a few minutes to days. In many cases, there is association with myotonia. Treatment, when necessary, involves intravenous administration of calcium gluconate and glucose. Diuretics such as acetazolamide and hydrochlorothiazide have shown benefits as preventive agents for new episodes.

RIGID PERSON SYNDROME: clinically characterized by axial muscle rigidity and contraction; slow progression of contraction to proximal muscles of the limbs; fixed deformity of the spine; presence of precipitated spasms

External stimulus; normal mental state; normal findings in motor and sensory nerves; Electroneuromyography with continuous motor activity with normal morphology, especially in paravertebral muscles, and continuous motor activity in antagonistic muscles, abolished during sleep, general anesthesia, and peripheral nerve block.

- ACQUIRED MYOPATHIES
- INFLAMMATORY MYOPATHIES
There is a large number of diseases considered of inflammatory origin. In some, the cause is known (virus, bacteria, protozoan, fungus), while in others, there is no specific etiological agent, possibly having an autoimmune basis.

- POLYMYOSITIS / DERMATOMYOSITIS
These are autoimmune diseases involving skeletal muscle tissue. In dermatomyositis, there is associated skin involvement. Diagnosis is based on clinical characteristics, supported by auxiliary examinations such as elevated serum CK and muscle biopsy with inflammatory and necrotic process. Treatment is done with the use of corticosteroids, or with immunosuppressants.

- ENDOCRINE MYOPATHIES
Muscle involvement is relatively frequent in endocrine diseases, most often incidentally and even imperceptibly clinically, or sometimes with predominant muscular involvement, allowing the underlying disease to be diagnosed.

- HYPERTHYROIDISM
It can manifest through 4 different clinical syndromes: thyroid toxic myopathy with chronic proximal muscle weakness; myasthenia; periodic paralysis, a very similar picture to hypocalcemic periodic paralysis; and exophthalmic ophthalmoplegia.

- HYPOTHYROIDISM
It can produce weakness, cramp, pain, and stiffness, as well as myotonia, reversible with hormonal replacement therapy.

- TOXIC MYOPATHIES
Muscle involvement related to the use of certain medications or drugs is not rare. Alcoholic myopathy, of chronic nature, characterized by proximal muscle weakness, is relatively frequent, but rarely limiting daily activities. However, acute alcoholic myopathy, characterized by pain and edema in lower extremities, or sometimes by generalized weakness due to rhabdomyolysis, is more severe. Treatment should be instituted as quickly as possible due to the risk of developing myoglobinuria and acute renal failure.

**PROJETO DE LEI Nº 1.657, DE 2011** (Do Sr. Alfredo Sirkis)

Acrescenta artigo à seção II, da Lei nº 9.605, de 1998, para vedar a distribuição e a comercialização de bebidas alcoólicas em embalagens plásticas e dá outras providências.

**O Congresso Nacional decreta:**

**Art. 1º** A Lei nº 9.605, de 12 de fevereiro de 1998, que “Dispõe sobre as sanções penais e administrativas derivadas de condutas e atividades lesivas ao meio ambiente, e dá outras providências”, passa a vigorar acrescida de art. 61-A com a seguinte redação:

“**Art. 61-A.** Distribuir e comercializar bebidas alcoólicas em embalagens de plástico, em qualquer dimensão.

**Pena – multa.**” (NR)

**Art. 3º** Esta lei entra em vigor após 60 dias de sua publicação oficial.

**Justificação**

O presente projeto de lei é a nossa segunda iniciativa tratando deste tema. Quando exerci o mandato de vereador da cidade do Rio de Janeiro conseguimos aprovar um projeto de lei que estabelece...

that "It is prohibited to distribute and market alcoholic beverages in plastic bottles (PET) of any size in the City of Rio de Janeiro." This initiative was transformed into Law No. 5,179 of 2010. The reasons that led us to present this proposal are even stronger at the national level.

The growth in the production of beverages in plastic bottles is today a major environmental problem, mainly due to river pollution, clogging of storm drains and water channels, causing floods and floods, and the long decomposition period of the material: approximately 400 (four hundred) years.

Brazil produces more than 11 (eleven) trillion plastic bottles annually, and the vast majority are discarded into the environment. With rare exceptions, these bottles end up in landfills, hindering the decomposition process of organic matter deposited there. It is worth noting that plastic bottles, including PET bottles, have their decomposition hindered because they impermeabilize certain layers of waste, preventing the circulation of gases and liquids.

However, instead of taking effective actions to recycle this material, the country is facing an increase of over 100% (one hundred percent) in the production of this material if the production of alcoholic beverages in plastic bottles is allowed. This means we are on the verge of doubling the number of units thrown into nature. For this reason, it is impossible to allow the production of alcoholic beverages in bottles, even of small size, as they easily enter storm drains and water channels due to their size.

The norm we propose with this bill follows the example of some countries that are well advanced in the treatment of their solid waste. In Europe, we can mention Denmark, which has already imposed barriers on the production of plastic bottles for alcoholic beverages for over a decade.

In this sense, I present this bill amending the Environmental Crimes Law to prohibit the distribution and marketing of alcoholic beverages in plastic packaging. In this way, I have no doubt that we will be making a significant contribution to the environment and improving the quality of life in cities. For the benefits of the proposal, I request the support of my fellow deputies for its approval.

Chamber of Sessions, June 22, 2011. - Deputy Alfredo Sirkis.
DIARY OF THE HOUSE OF DEPUTIES

**Article 2**
This Law enters into force on the date of its publication, producing effects from January 1st of the following year.

**Justification**
The legislation of the Individual Income Tax (IRPF) establishes a tax incidence table applied to the income of the taxpayer and his dependents, including spouses, partners, and companions. When the taxpayer decides to file a joint annual return, the incomes of the entire family unit are summed without any alteration in the progressive table values.

Income refers to the set of individuals who make up the family nucleus, but the table refers to the income of a single taxpayer.

This methodology produces significant distortions in tax payment. A couple, where one spouse receives R$ 2,390.00 monthly and the other R$ 600.00, has a combined monthly income of R$ 2,990.00. Ignoring deductions, the first spouse collects approximately R$ 155.00 monthly, which amounts to a family expenditure of roughly R$ 1,860.00 on income tax at the end of the year. Another couple, where both spouses receive R$ 1,495.00, do not pay any income tax, although their family income is exactly the same as the previous couple.

This is a distortion of our tax legislation. In accordance with the principle of equality, families with the same income should pay the same amount of income tax.

With the aim of correcting this anomaly, we are proposing that the tax incidence ranges of the IRPF table, both monthly and annual, be doubled when a couple opts to offer their incomes for taxation jointly.

This joint family taxation would also be advantageous in cases where one of the spouses becomes unemployed or stops working to dedicate themselves fully to studies or even to caring for a newly born or adopted child.

Finally, in a matter of justice, I must register that this proposal resulted from a contribution by Mr. Henrique Toledo, an advertising professional residing in Goiânia, GO.

For the aforementioned reasons, we count on the support of the Ladies and Gentlemen Parliamentarians for the improvement and approval of this initiative.

Chamber of Sessions, June 22, 2011. – João Campos, Federal Deputy.

LEGISLATIVE DECREE PROJECT
NO. 312, OF 2011
(By Mr. Roberto de Lucena and Mr. João Campos)
Suspends the application of the decision of the
Supreme Federal Court rendered in Argument of
Fundamental Precept Breach (ADPF) 187, which
recognizes the constitutionality of the so-called
"Marijuana March."
The National Congress decrees:
Article 1. The decision of the Supreme Federal
Court rendered in Argument of Fundamental
Precept Breach (ADPF) 187, which recognizes the
constitutionality of the so-called "Marijuana March,"
is hereby suspended.
Article 2. This legislative decree shall enter into
force on the date of its publication.
Justification
OF THE STF DECISION
On June 15, 2011, the Supreme Federal Court
accepted, in a decision rendered in Argument of
Fundamental Precept Breach (ADPF) 187, which
recognizes the constitutionality of the so-called
"Marijuana March."
The STF, under the pretext of interpreting that
Article 287 of the Penal Code has occasionally been
interpreted by the Judiciary to consider so-called
pro-legalization of marijuana marches as an
incitement to crime, following the vote of the
relator, Minister Celso de Mello, the Court gave a
constitutional interpretation to the Penal Code
provision to distance any understanding that the
marches constitute an incitement to crime. For the
ministers present at the session, freedom of
expression and assembly prevails in these cases.
The aforementioned decision, due to its legal
nature, has a binding effect and reaches the entire
society.
In less technical language, it means that,
following the said decision, the gathering of pro-
legalization of marijuana and other narcotic groups
can be held without characterizing it as an
incitement to crime.
The highest body of the Judiciary has ruled
that Article 287 of the Brazilian Penal Code,
incitement to crime, does not apply in the case of
pro-marijuana marches:
"Article 287. Publicly making an apology
of a criminal fact or of a criminal author.
Penalty: - Detention, from 3 (three) to 6 (six)
months, or fine."
In view of similar facts, the Judicial Authorities
of several states of the Federation have suspended

"Marijuana March" that had taken place in previous years
in several cities. In the State of Rio de Janeiro, Judge Roberto Câmara Lacé Brandão cites in his decision
the argument of the Public Ministry that "the situation
initially presented as a peaceful political manifestation,
in truth masks an orchestrated action through the spread
of drug consumption," which "would constitute the crime
of advocating drug trafficking."

Freedom cannot be confused with liberation, advocating a criminal act, and preaching free speech without respecting the existing legal order. Therefore, freedom of expression has legal and moral limits.

The main objective of the march is the advocacy of the use of narcotics, and once anonymous, it conflicts with a legal provision, as affirmed by the distinguished Judge of the Court of Justice of the State of São Paulo, Dr. Maria Tereza do Amaral:

"It is not unknown the constitutional right to freedom of expression and assembly,
which, obviously, is not being violated in this case,
since it is not a debate of ideas but a public manifestation
of the collective use of marijuana."

It is important to note that the STF (Supreme Court of Brazil) created the aforementioned right
on the grounds of exercising the competence established by Article 102, Item I, Subitem "a," of the Federal Constitution,
in its role as guardian of the Magna Carta.

Article 102 - The Supreme Federal Court shall, primarily, safeguard the Constitution,
and shall: (we have emphasized)

I - originally process and judge:
a) direct actions of unconstitutionality of federal or state laws or normative acts,
and actions declaring the constitutionality of federal laws or normative acts; (we have emphasized)

VIOLATION OF THE COMPETENCE OF THE LEGISLATIVE POWER

This Legislative Decree Project aims to revoke, based on the competence of the National Congress, as established in Items V and XI of Article 49 of the Federal Constitution,
the effects of the decision of the Supreme Federal Court in Argument on the Violation of a Fundamental Precept (ADPF) No. 187,
which recognized the free manifestation of the "Marijuana March."

Without delving into the merits of the issue, it is observed from the examination and analysis of the controversial decision's text
that the Supreme Federal Court exceeded its power to interpret a constitutional norm, as established by Item I, Subitem "a," of Article 102 of the CF.
DIARY OF THE HOUSE OF DEPUTIES

Effectively, the disputed decision invades the
competence of the Legislative Power, because it alters
a provision of the Penal Code, a situation that can only
occur through a law, in both formal and material senses,
consisting of a general and abstract norm of conduct,
enacted by the Legislative and sanctioned by the Execu-
tive, in accordance with the principle of legality as estab-
lished in Article 5, Clause II, of the Federal Constitution.
Article 5 ...
II – No one shall be obliged to do or refrain from do-
ing anything but in accordance with the law; (we have
emphasized)
This means, in simpler terms, that the legislator
should make laws, the judge should decide, and the ad-
ministrator should execute.
The discussed decision also violated the theory of the
separation of powers, established in Article 2 of the Mag-
na Carta.
Article 2 – The Union's powers, independent and har-
monious among themselves, are the Legislative, the Ex-
ecutive, and the Judicial. (we have emphasized)
The decision in question usurped the Union's attri-
bution, which is to legislate exclusively on criminal law,
as provided in Article 22, Clause I, of the CF.
Article 22 – It is the Union's exclusive competence to
legislate on:
I – civil, commercial, penal, procedural, electoral,
agrarian, maritime, aeronautic, space, and labor law. (we
have emphasized)
Moreover, the incorrect judgment of the STF (Supre-
me Court) altered the text of Article 287 of the Penal Code,
which normally would depend on a legislating process
aimed at testing a law project, through a simple decision.
Incidentally, it is important to distinguish the activity
of interpreting the law, attributed to the Judicial Power,
from the task of creating law, conferred upon the Legisla-
tive Power.
According to the Aulete dictionary, interpret means:
to give meaning, explain a word, text, law, etc. On the
other hand, create means: to give existence, origin, con-
cept.
Undeniably, when the STF granted full freedom to
organize pro-cannabis marches without characterizing
apology for crime, it exceeded the limits of interpreting
the constitutional norm, creating a new law.
ON THE DEFENSE OF THE LEGISLATIVE POWER'S
COMPETENCE
Clauses V and XI of Article 49 of the Political Charter
provide that it is the National Congress's exclusive com-
petence to safeguard its legislative competence in the
face of the normative attribution of the other Powers.
