segments.text:
Article 49. It is the exclusive competence of the National Congress:

...

V – to annul normative acts of the Executive Branch that exceed its regulatory power or the limits of legislative delegation;

XI – to ensure the preservation of its legislative competence in the face of the normative attribution of the other Powers; (I have emphasized)

The above-described chart clearly demonstrates that the Judicial Power has invaded the sphere of competence of the Legislative Power.

The Legislative Power is the only competent entity to create rights and obligations in interpersonal relations. This means that no other authority, no matter how respected, has the competence to legislate in its place, under penalty of usurpation of powers.

The competence of the Federal Supreme Court to interpret constitutional norms cannot be understood as a prerogative to amend the Penal Code, much less as a competence to innovate in the legislative field.

It is important to emphasize that the competence provided for in Article 49, Clause XI, of the Federal Constitution, has the nature of a true political control of constitutionality, as the decisions made by the Judicial Power that exceed its attributes contradict the rules of competence established by the Magna Carta.

On this subject, Montesquieu already warned that "it is an eternal experience that whoever holds power tends to abuse it."

Therefore, it is indispensable that power be held by power. Confrontation may occur, which would be regrettable for democracy, which is precisely being corrupted by those who hold the competence to restore the legal order when harmed, but not to create obligations, duties, rights, and powers contrary to the legislator.

ON THE POSSIBILITY OF SUSPENDING THE EFFECTS OF JUDICIAL ACTS

Thus, it is for the National Congress, in ensuring the preservation of its legislative competence, to use the remedy attributed to it by Article 49, Clause XI, of the Federal Constitution, in analogy with the prerogative conferred by Clause V of the same article.

There is no doubt that if the Legislative Power can annul the effects of abusive acts of the Executive Branch, in order to fulfill its prerogative of ensuring the preservation of its legislative competence, the same remedy should be extended to this House to suspend the illegal acts of the Judicial Power, without
DIARY OF THE HOUSE OF DEPUTIES

segments.text:
Within the framework of granting the constitutional norm the necessary effectiveness to achieve the objectives of the constituent power, including the principle of separation of powers.

It is worth remembering that the interpretation of the Constitution cannot be carried out through an isolated analysis of one of its provisions, but according to the entire legal order established by it, under penalty of ineffectiveness.

In the present case, if it is not possible to annul the effects of a decision that exceeded the jurisdiction of the judiciary, the legal order and the independence of the powers will be affected, and consequently, the very constitutional order.

In reality, the possibility for the legislative power to suspend the effects of abusive acts of the judiciary is part of the system of checks and balances, essential to the mechanism of separation of powers proposed by Montesquieu during the French Revolution.

To this end, the Federal Constitution establishes a complex mechanism of reciprocal controls among the three powers, so that at the same time, one power controls the others and is controlled by them.

**CONCLUSION**

Therefore, it is concluded that the National Congress should adopt the measures that are due to it to maintain the harmony in our legal order, using the remedy granted to it by articles 49, paragraphs V and XI, of the Federal Constitution, against such usurpations, under penalty of undermining democracy and breaking down the nation's legal system, with the establishment of odious legal absolutism.

Convinced of the arguments presented here, we submit this Legislative Decree Project, in the zeal of the legislative competence and also with a preventive character regarding other decisions that the Supreme Federal Court may issue in the future, laden with unlimited judicial activism that constitutes an invasion of the legislative competence.

In the light of all that has been said, we count on the support of the noble Peers to approve this Legislative Decree Project, with the aim of suspending the decision of the Supreme Federal Court in the Fundamental Precept Violation (ADPF) 187, which recognized the constitutionality of the so-called "Cannabis March," annulling all acts derived from it.

# APPEAL No. 57, 2011
(From Mr. Mauro Nazif)
Appeal against the President of the CD's denial of the Project of Law No. 1476/2011

Mr. President,
Based on Article 137, § 2 of the Internal Regulation of the Chamber of Deputies - RICD, I come before Your Excellency to file an APPEAL to the Plenary of Your decision that denied liminarly the follow-up to Project of Law No. 1476/2011 on the argument that it contains matters of exclusive initiative of the President of the Republic, as per the provisions of Article 61, § 1, II, “a” and “c” of the Federal Constitution, in accordance with the following factual and legal guidelines.

Law No. 12.277/2010 restructured the remuneration structure of several careers in the federal administration. However, due to a failure in the list of careers benefited by the so-called Special Remuneration Structure, we proposed its correction precisely through the Project of Law in question. Therefore, we included the

In this structure, due to the right that is his, including one due by nature, the administrator, unfortunately, Your Excellency prematurely stopped the proposal we presented to rectify this defect, communicated to us through Ofício 907/2011/SGM/P.

In fact, the constitutional devices mentioned establish exclusive legislative initiative of the President of the Republic for matters related to federal public servants. Meanwhile, if this is true, it is no less true that perhaps we are interpreting these devices in an extremely radical manner. After all, the bill in question does not create positions, jobs, or functions in the public administration, nor does it institute, revoke, or alter any legal regime, system of appointment of positions, stability, and retirement for any category of public servants.

Let us examine the constitutional devices:

"Article 61. .................................................

a) the creation of public positions, functions, or jobs in the direct and autonomous administration or the increase of their remuneration;

The PL No. 1476/2011, which we presented, addresses a terrible flaw that is vehemently challenging the principle, also of constitutional stature, of equality. It merely promotes the inclusion of a specific category of servants - administrators - in the Special Remunerary Structure that is already contained in Law No. 12.277/2010. Note Your Excellency that the legal regime - precisely, the Special Remunerary Structure - is already established; that public positions of the various careers that make up this Structure are already established; that the system of appointment of positions, stability, and retirement is also already established. Everything is already defined and established by Law No. 12.277/2010.

In this context, how can the PL No. 1.476/2011 mistreat the subclauses "a" and "c" of the aforementioned Constitutional Article? How, if subclause "a" mentions "creation" of positions and functions and subclause "c" refers to "legal regime," "appointment," "stability," and "retirement"? By inserting the category of administrators into the legal regime - forgive the audacity of this Parliamentarian, Mr. President, but we insist on Your Opinion - but we insist on Your Opinion...

Previously, if we are not so radical in the interpretation of such provisions, we will realize that PL No. 1476 does not contain any constitutional vice of exclusive legislative initiative. The relevant PL only acquires the vice of initiative if we take the interpretation of the aforementioned clauses to the extreme, to the last consequences. But, as we know, extremes, of any side, are not good, as they can nullify and obscure a legitimate prerogative of the private or public agent, mostly the political agent, as we are all, Honorable President. It is not for another reason that the Romans, from the high chair of their millennium-old and still unsurpassed practice of jurisprudence, advocated that "IN MEDIO EST VIRTUS," that is, virtue is in the middle path.

If we continue with this radicality in interpretation, how will we reconcile Article 61, which provides for exclusive initiative, with Article 44, both of the Constitution, which states that the legislative power belongs to - and only to - the National Congress? Truly, if it is true that the President has the initiative to determine certain norms, it is precisely because of Article 44 that we, within the internal framework of Parliament, can propose the necessary amendments, subject to some hypotheses, to such norms. Taking the provisions of Article 61 to the last consequences would mean saying that a parliamentarian could not, even, amend the respective projects of exclusive initiative, not only of the President, but also, for example, of the Superior Courts.

However, this would mean nullifying the provisions of Article 44 of the Constitution. As we know, there cannot be unconstitutionality within the Constitution itself. If this is true, we must admit some tempering in the interpretation, in order to reconcile Article 61 with the provisions of Article 44. Thus, we must admit that if we were facing the legislative process of Law No. 12.277/2010, this parliamentarian could very well propose amendments to the then draft law. There is no reasonable and ponderable reason to say that this parliamentarian could not then propose a law project that has the same effect and function as an amendment that could be presented in the procedural-regimental tramit of Law No. 12.277/2010. Without altering the substance, the merit and the essence of the project that would result in Law No. 12.277/2010, the amendment (as the draft law now presented) would serve to correct a situation that is in every way offensive to the principle of equality, which is a constitutional guarantee.

The indication would be the path that, of all, would precisely overlap exclusive initiative (Article 61) with the capacity and

To the legislative fitness of the members of this National Congress (art. 44), an overlap with which we could, with humility, agree. The Constitution is a system, and if it is a system, there cannot be predominance of one over the other, but rather harmonization between the various constitutional provisions. Humility compels us to strive for the harmonization of the various constitutional mandates.

For all the reasons stated, the Deputy, now Appellant, requests that Your Excellency, upon recognizing this Appeal, given its full timeliness, grant it for the specific purpose of, by revoking your order of suspension, allowing the free flow of Law Project No. 1476/2011, of our authorship, in the interest of justice, not only for this Parliament, but equally for the Brazilian People, who, with kindness, have ceded us their legislative capacity.

Justification

On April 20, 2010, this parliamentarian received from the First Secretariat the responses from Minister of Defense, Dr. Nelson Jobim, to the Information Request of the Chamber No. 4470 of 2009 (RIC 4470/2009), through Ofício 4225-GM/Aspar-MD, regarding the diligences carried out in response to public information requests submitted to the Civil House of the Presidency of the Republic and six other ministries, including the Ministry of Defense, by scholars of the UFO phenomenon. The petitioners had invoked the Law 11.111/2005 at the end of 2007, but two years later, the demand had not been fully met. Given the delay of that ministry in applying legal directives, the commission formed by scholars of this controversial phenomenon, even recognized by our Brazilian Air Force, requested our intervention with this Legislative House to request speed and full attention to their request, which was initially done through the aforementioned request.

Based on the responses of Mr. Minister, specifically the affirmations that “all documents related to the subject (UFO) that had some degree of secrecy were declassified due to the legal time limit,” that the Center for Documentation and History of the Brazilian Air Force (CENDOC) is the overall responsible for this subject in his Ministry, and that it would close on August 31, 2010, the remittance of its entire archive to the Regional Coordination of the National Archive in the Federal District (COREG), it was noticed, after the end of this stipulated term, the persistence of several pending matters, as well as the emergence of new demands. And more, it was detected what was already presumed, that is, that neither

All that was requested by the CBU as early as 2007 would—as it was not—have been sent to that Authority. Therefore, a significant portion of the gaps already detected and questioned in RIC 4470/2009 remained absent from the declassified document lots. Even if the Minister made the above statements, there are consistent historical documentary indications that contradict them. The indications and research put into practice by independent UFO phenomenon researchers point to the fact that, when all the information is compared, the actions of the Armed Forces Commands do not validate the statements of their supreme commander.

During much of the 1950s, particularly within the short and tumultuous Government of Café Filho (1954/55), several UFO-related events marked those years deeply. To such an extent that then Air Force Minister, Brigadier Eduardo Gomes, established the "Commission for the Investigation of Flying Saucers," and appointed Brigadier João Adil de Oliveira as its head. The latter reported, at an event of the Superior War School, with the presence of technicians, journalists, and scientists, as well as the High Command of the Armed Forces, including the Chief of the EMFA, the positive results and conclusions of that important Commission. There is no doubt that Brig. Oliveira attested to the reality of UFOs. Neither the documents of this Commission, nor information about this ESG lecture, were included in the documentation of that decade, now found in the National Archive. The same happened with other Air Force information, which, despite being of restricted knowledge, and in some cases public, inexplicably were not sent to COREG.

A shocking example, detected as early as 2008 and demanded in RIC 4470/2009, was the lack of response to the full disclosure of information regarding the most famous of all military incursions into the action of supposedly extraterrestrial creatures in the Brazilian airspace, Operation Prato. What is surprising is that on August 10th of last year, the Air Force admitted and officially opened part of its procedure scheme regarding the UFO issue, through the publication in the DOU of Portaria 551/GC3. However, these procedures did not include the sending to the National Archive of the bulk of the information from the said Operation. Although FAB was the most inclined to discuss the opening of the requested information by ufologists, the nebulous situation regarding the size of its files and how far the Command is willing to cede persists.

They would often encounter him on their way, and they would never run away if they saw him, unlike when they spotted the strange and foul-smelling creature. The students even compared the being to "the Devil," and all of them categorically denied it being Mudinho.

Vittorio Pacaccini, a scholar of the case and author of the book that sparked the IPM, was one of the first people to learn of the Army's final version explaining the creature, and he quickly dismantled it, stating that "the comparison is an insult to the intelligence of the witnesses and Luis' family, the Mudinho." Incidentally, this was not the first version given by the EsSA officers to explain a creature seen in the morning of January 20, 1996, and again in the afternoon. REQUEST FOR INFORMATION
No. 680, 2011
(From Mr. Antonio Carlos Mendes Thame)
Requests from the Most Excellent Minister of Mines and Energy, Mr. Edison Lobão,
information regarding the Abreu de Lima Refinery project in the Brazilian state of Pernambuco,
and concerning the contractual relations between Petrobras and the Venezuelan state-owned
company PDVSA – Petróleo de Venezuela S.A.
Mr. President,
Based on Article 50 of the Federal Constitution, and Articles 115, paragraph I, and 116 of the
Internal Rules of the Chamber of Deputies, I request that Your Excellency direct the Minister
of State for Mines and Energy, Mr. Edison Lobão, to provide information regarding the Abreu
de Lima Refinery project in the Brazilian state of Pernambuco, and concerning the contractual
relations between Petrobras and the Venezuelan state-owned company PDVSA – Petróleo de
Venezuela S.A.
In this regard, we request that the Minister of State for Mines and Energy provide the
following information:
Why does Brazil maintain – or reserve – a 40% participation in the Abreu de Lima Refinery
project in the state of Pernambuco for the Venezuelan state-owned company PDVSA, even
though Petrobras has already built 35% of the project on its own?
What measures does the constitutive contract of the Abreu de Lima Refinery provide for in
the event of a financial contribution default by a shareholder?
In response to the default by PDVSA of its contribution corresponding to its participation in
the Abreu de Lima Refinery, what actions have been taken by this Ministry? Have notices
regarding contractual default been issued? Does the default provide for fines or other
penalties?
Under what circumstances, or circumstances, should this Ministry denounce the
cancellation of the association?
If PDVSA cancels or withdraws its participation in the aforementioned project, will
Petrobras implement it without a foreign partner?
What is the US$ 1.4 billion debt of PDVSA to Petrobras? When did it expire?
Do(es) the contract(s) provide guarantees for situations of default by PDVSA? What kind?
Do(es) the contract(s) provide for fines and other penalties for delays?

Does the contract provide for the suspension of services? If so, what facts might lead to such an attitude and under what conditions will it be adopted?

What values have been added to the referred debt due to interest and fees on the overdue amounts?

What procedures has Petrobras adopted regarding the overdue amounts? If these procedures have not yet been adopted, why not? When will they be implemented?

Justification

The enormous social debt of the Brazilian state, of which economic experts, social policies, and all instances of political power speak, has placed, with prominent relevance, the lack of public resources to meet the needs of interventions by municipal, state, and federal governments to reverse shortages.

In the opposite direction of initiatives that could materialize the elimination of this recognized social debt, the government of President Dilma Rousseff demonstrates its intention to maintain the same external policy of her predecessor, based on acts of generosity with Union money, in particular to Latin American governments with which it shares ideological affinities.

During a recent visit to Brazil, Venezuelan President Hugo Chávez obtained promises from his colleague Dilma Rousseff for a BNDES loan of US$ 637 million to the powerful state-owned oil company PDVSA to finance a shipyard in the state of Sucre with the participation of Brazilian investors who will also allocate US$ 4 billion in a fund intended to finance infrastructure projects in Venezuela.

According to information disclosed by the Brazilian press, the same state-owned PDVSA owes Petrobras approximately US$ 1.4 billion, corresponding to services provided by the Brazilian state in Venezuelan oil fields. To date, PDVSA has not contributed the corresponding resources for its 40% participation in the Abreu de Lima Refinery project in Pernambuco, whose negotiations have dragged on since 2005.

Instead of invoking the contractual safeguards that usually regulate contracts involving substantial public resources, especially in projects with foreign investors' participation, the Brazilian government chose to be lenient with the defaulting Venezuelan government and ordered the execution of the Abreu de Lima Refinery works without the money of the supposed partner. Approximately
DIARY OF THE HOUSE OF DEPUTIES

Thirty-five percent of the work has already been completed
under the exclusive financial responsibility of Petrobras.
Even if the Venezuelan government appears with
the agreed funds in the new deadline granted - in
August of this year - the Brazilian government owes
explanations to both society and this National Congress
regarding such leniency.
The promise of the President of Brazil - which corresponds
to a commitment of the entire people she represents -
of a new BNDES loan to Venezuela without that country
having presented acceptable guarantees for the release
of the previous loan intended to finance its participation
in the Pernambuco Refinery is a decision that goes against
technical logic.
This procedure of our country's government involves
the use of Union money and not just the exchange of
goodwill statements between the parties regarding the
closening of relations between the two countries.
However, it is not a matter of invoking
Article 70 and the clauses that make up Article 71 of
the Federal Constitution, which deal with "Continuous
Financial and Budgetary Oversight", but rather to examine
these issues in the light of the statement of Article 85
which deals with transparency and "Responsibility of
the President of the Republic" regarding probity in
administration, as well as the principles of "legality,
impersonality, morality, publicity and efficiency"
established in Article 37.

Instead of invoking the contractual safeguards that typically regulate operations contracts,

that information be requested from the Minister of State for Justice, Mr. José Eduardo Martins Cardozo, regarding recent legislative measures taken by the governments of Paraguay and Bolivia that facilitate the registration of vehicles in an irregular situation in those countries, many of which are products of crimes committed in Brazil. - Does the Brazilian government have information provided by the Bolivian government regarding the number of irregular vehicles circulating in Bolivian territory?

- Based on records in crime reports, what is the estimated fleet of Brazilian vehicles stolen and circulating in Paraguay?

- What numbers and trends do the statistics of stolen vehicles in Brazil and taken to Paraguay present?

Stolen in these border areas (Bolivia and Paraguay) in the last ten years?

Justification

Smuggling, theft, and robbery of vehicles, which only intensify in two of the most active and threatening sections of the vast Brazilian border, have been transformed into profitable economic activities by the neighboring countries Bolivia and Paraguay. Decisions by the governments of these two countries created mechanisms that enable the regularization of fleets of stolen vehicles circulating within their territories, thus incorporating criminal products into sources of tax revenue.

Paraguayan law exempts its police from investigating the provenance of vehicles, but allows the former owner to visit the country to prove that the asset belonged to them. Bolivian law says nothing about investigation. It simply charges a fee to grant registration without any reference to the possibility of investigation or recovery of the asset.

Both cases reflect unilateral decisions by the neighboring governments, given that the illicit activities that accumulate in these locations are known, as well as the alleged difficulties of the systems

repressives aimed at confronting criminal organizations that take advantage of the vastness of borders – 15,719 kilometers with ten countries – and often use a larger number of operators, flexible tactical schemes, and cutting-edge technological resources to evade surveillance systems.

These events underscore the strategic importance of Brazil's relations with its neighbors.

Bolivia is among those suggesting additional relationship policies due to the countless transit possibilities along the dividing line that separates it and also connects it to Brazilian territory.

The legalization in that country of stolen vehicles is not an isolated incident in the list of decisions contrary to Brazil's interests. It becomes urgent to ask what the Brazilian government is waiting for to react in accordance with the guidelines governing the principles of cooperation between nations.

First, Evo Morales ordered the invasion and occupation of Petrobras facilities with military troops and seized them through illegal acts, maintaining military occupation for approximately 30 days.

Instead of reacting and challenging the bravado of the neighboring president in international courts, then-President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva condescended and, extravagantly, not only omitted the expressions of rejection that Brazilians expected from him, but also attempted to downplay the gravity of the events with an exotic declaration of recognition of Bolivian sovereignty.

The Brazilian government's lassitude in the face of the appropriation (sequestration) of Petrobras facilities emboldened Evo Morales' already weakened leadership, encouraging him to expand his gains (sic). A continuous series of pressures – announced during his election campaign – began for an increase in gas prices, breaking the agreements that made it possible to build the gas pipeline between the two countries.

Petrobras was reluctant, understanding, according to the advice of its legal counsel, that Morales' demand for additional payment was illegal. Morales radicalized, threatened to cut off gas supplies, and again obtained an addendum to the import contract that will inject additional gains of US$ 1.2 billion into Bolivian coffers over the next few years.

At no point did Brazilian government authorities inform what legal arrangement was used to overturn Petrobras' contrary opinion, allowing Morales to achieve another victory over Brazil.

Morales. The government's motivation was the water levels in the hydroelectric reservoirs.

By the end of the same Friday, after meeting with Bolivian ministers, Lobão announced, contrary to what he had stated in the morning, that Brazil "will increase" - not reduce - the volume of purchases of Bolivian gas.

This episode could well symbolize the end of a process of troubled bilateral relations from the end of the previous government and the beginning of a reorientation of the country's foreign policy in the direction of pragmatism historically adopted by Itamaraty.

However, Evo Morales' decision to legalize the fleet of cars that circulate irregularly on Bolivian territory, composed mostly of vehicles stolen in Brazil, has not yet produced the appropriate responses from the Brazilian government.

According to information from the newspaper O Estado de S.Paulo, in its edition of June 14, 2011, page 3,

"The situation is particularly delicate in Mato Grosso, which has 953 km of border with Bolivia, 750 km of dry border, in urban and rural areas. There, 2,568 vehicle thefts and 2,030 robberies were recorded in 2010. In addition, it is through Mato Grosso that stolen cars from other states cross the borders. The commander of the Special Frontier Group, which operates in municipalities bordering Bolivia, informs that 300 vehicles were recovered in 2010, but if Morales persists in granting amnesty to criminals, the recovery of cars will be compromised."

The silence of the Brazilian government leads to the assumption that measures such as the legalization of stolen vehicles by Evo Morales also fall within the reservation made by Lula when, in 2006, he authorized the military invasion of Petrobras refineries in Bolivia: a matter of national sovereignty.

REQUEST FOR INFORMATION
No. 684, of 2011
(Mr. Antonio Carlos Mendes Thame)
Requests from the most honorable Minister of Foreign Affairs, Mr. Antonio de Aguiar Patriota, information regarding recent legislative measures of the governments of Paraguay and Bolivia that facilitate the registration of vehicles in an irregular situation in those countries, many of which are products of crimes committed in Brazil.

Mr. President,

Based on Article 50 of the Federal Constitution, and Article 115, paragraph I, and 116 of the Internal Regulation of the Chamber of Deputies, I request that Your Excellency order the Minister of State for Foreign Affairs, Mr. Antonio de Aguiar Patriota, to provide information on recent legislative measures of the governments of Paraguay and Bolivia that facilitate the registration of vehicles in an irregular situation in those countries, many of which are products of crimes committed in Brazil.

In this regard, we request that the Minister of State for Foreign Affairs provide the following information:

- Does the Brazilian government have information provided by the Bolivian government regarding the number of irregular vehicles circulating in Bolivian territory?
- Does the Brazilian government have information provided by the Paraguayan government regarding the number of irregular vehicles circulating in Paraguayan territory?
- Based on records in crime reports, what is the estimated fleet of Brazilian vehicles stolen and circulating in Bolivia?
- Based on records in crime reports, what is the estimated fleet of Brazilian vehicles stolen and circulating in Paraguay?
- What is the expected impact by the Federal and Highway Police with the implementation of the regularization adopted by Bolivia?
- What is the expected impact by the Federal and Highway Police with the implementation of the regularization adopted by Paraguay?
- What is the evaluation of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs regarding the measures of "nationalization" (sic) adopted by Bolivia and Paraguay?
- Are other countries that share a border with Bolivia and Paraguay facing the same problem?
- Do Colombia, Venezuela, Suriname, Guyana, French Guiana, Argentina, Uruguay, and Peru discuss or implement similar measures?

Do they tend to adopt measures similar to those of Paraguay and Bolivia?
– What numbers and what trend do the statistics of stolen vehicles in Brazil that are taken to Bolivia show?
– What numbers and what trend do the statistics of stolen vehicles in Brazil that are taken to Paraguay show?
– What numbers and trend do the statistics of recovered stolen vehicles in the border areas with Bolivia show?
– What numbers and trend do the statistics of recovered stolen vehicles in the border areas with Paraguay show?
– What measures has the Brazilian government been taking to combat thefts and recover stolen vehicles in these border areas (Bolivia and Paraguay) over the past ten years?
– In its action or reaction plans to the measures adopted by Bolivia and Paraguay, will Brazil act alone or seek the collaboration of these countries? How?
– Have the governments of Bolivia and Paraguay collaborated with Brazilian authorities in this area? How?
– If they do not collaborate, why not?
– Do the Federal and Road Polices have legal instruments that regulate their activities regarding controls and investigations by the governments of Bolivia and Paraguay?
– If so, what is the legal basis that underpins them?
– Does Brazil have criminal cooperation agreements with these two countries?
– If so, what are the main provisions for information exchange and supporting actions intended for the parties?
– If not, why have they not been negotiated and implemented, given that diplomatic relations between countries with a common border presuppose the existence of such agreements?
– If such agreements exist, are they in line with MERCOSUR? If so, how are they harmonized?
– If not, why has Brazil not yet tabled this proposal to that body?

Decisions of the governments of these two countries created mechanisms that enable the regularization of fleets of stolen vehicles circulating within their territories, thereby incorporating criminal products into tax revenue sources.

Paraguayan law exempts its police from investigating the provenance of vehicles, but allows the former owner to visit the country to prove that the asset belonged to them.

Bolivian law says nothing about investigation. It simply charges a fee to grant registration without any reference to the possibility of investigation or recovery of the asset.

Both cases reflect unilateral decisions of the neighboring governments, given the known illicit activities that accumulate in these areas, as well as the alleged difficulties of repressive systems intended to confront criminal organizations that take advantage of the vastness of borders—15,719 kilometers with ten countries—and often employ more operators, flexible tactical schemes, and cutting-edge technological resources to evade surveillance systems.

These events underscore the strategic importance of Brazil's relations with its neighbors.

Bolivia is among those suggesting additional relationship policies due to the countless transit possibilities along the dividing line that separates it and also connects it to Brazilian territory.

The legalization in that country of stolen vehicles is not an isolated incident in the list of decisions contrary to Brazil's interests. It becomes urgent to ask what the Brazilian government is waiting for to react in accordance with the guidelines governing the principles of cooperation between nations.

REQUEST FOR INFORMATION
No. 685, 2011
(From Mr. Antonio Carlos Mendes Thame)
Request that the Minister of State for Mines and Energy provide information
regarding the Abreu de Lima Refinery in Pernambuco, Brazil, in response to the following questions.
Mr. President:
Based on Article 50, § 2, of the Federal Constitution, and Articles 115 and 116 of the Internal Regulation,
I request, after consulting the Desk, that the following information be requested from the Minister
of State for Mines and Energy regarding the Abreu de Lima Refinery in Pernambuco, Brazil, in response
to the following questions:
- Why does Brazil maintain - or reserve - a 40% stake in the Abreu de Lima Refinery project in the
state of Pernambuco for the state-owned Venezuelan company, PDVSA, even though Petrobras has already
built 35% of the project alone?
- What measures does the constitutive contract of the Abreu de Lima Refinery provide for in the
event of a financial contribution failure by a shareholder?
- In light of PDVSA's failure to contribute the corresponding resources for its participation in the
Abreu de Lima Refinery, what actions has this Ministry taken? Have notices regarding contractual
breach been issued? Does the breach provide for fines or other penalties?
- Under what circumstances, or circumstances, should this Ministry denounce the cancellation of
the association?
- If PDVSA withdraws or abandons its participation in the project, will Petrobras implement it without
a foreign partner?
- What is the US$ 1.4 billion debt that PDVSA owes to Petrobras? When did it expire?
- Does the contract provide for guarantees in the event of PDVSA's default? What guarantees?
- Does the contract provide for fines and other penalties for delays?
- Does the contract provide for the suspension of services? If so, what facts could lead to such a
decision and under what conditions will it be implemented?

– What values have been added to the outstanding debt due to interest and fees on the overdue amounts?
– What procedures has Petrobras adopted regarding the overdue amounts? If these procedures have not yet been implemented, why not? When will they be?

Justification
The enormous social debt of the Brazilian state, of which economic experts, social policy specialists, and all branches of the political power speak, has placed, with prominent relevance, the lack of public resources to address the needs of interventions by municipal, state, and federal governments to reverse these deficiencies.

In the opposite direction of initiatives that could materialize the elimination of this recognized social debt, the government of President Dilma Rousseff demonstrates its intention to maintain the same external policy of her predecessor, based on acts of generosity with Union funds, particularly towards Latin American governments with which it shares ideological affinities.

During a recent visit to Brazil, Venezuelan President Hugo Chávez received promises from his Brazilian counterpart, Dilma Rousseff, for a BNDES loan of US$ 637 million to the powerful state-owned oil company PDVSA to finance a shipyard in the state of Sucre with the participation of Brazilian investors who will also allocate US$ 4 billion in a fund intended to finance infrastructure projects in Venezuela.

According to information disclosed by the Brazilian press, the same state-owned PDVSA owes Petrobras approximately US$ 1.4 billion, corresponding to services provided by the Brazilian state in Venezuelan oil fields. To date, PDVSA has not contributed the corresponding resources for its 40% participation in the Abreu de Lima Refinery project in Pernambuco, whose negotiations have been dragging on since 2005.

Instead of invoking the contractual safeguards that usually regulate contracts involving substantial public resources, especially in projects with foreign investor participation, the Brazilian government chose to be lenient with the defaulting Venezuelan government and ordered the execution of the Abreu de Lima Refinery works without the money of the supposed partner. Approximately 35% of the works have already been carried out at the exclusive financial expense of Petrobras.
DIARY OF THE HOUSE OF DEPUTIES

Even though the Venezuelan government appears with
the money agreed upon in the new deadline granted—
in August of this year—the Brazilian government owes
explanations to both society and this National Congress
regarding such leniency.
The promise of the President of Brazil—which corresponds
to a commitment of the entire people she represents—
for a new BNDES loan to Venezuela without that country
having presented acceptable guarantees for the release
of the previous loan intended to finance its participation
in the Pernambuco Refinery is a decision that goes against
technical logic.
This procedure of our country's government involves
the use of Union money and not just the exchange of
goodwill statements between the parties regarding the
closening of relations between the two countries.
However, it is not a matter of invoking Article 70 and
the clauses that make up Article 71 of the Federal
Constitution, which deal with "Continuous Financial
and Budgetary Oversight," but rather to examine these
issues in the light of the statement in Article 85, which
deals with transparency and "Responsibility of the
President of the Republic" regarding probity in adminis-
tration, as well as the principles of "legality, impar-
tiality, morality, publicity, and efficiency" established
in Article 37.
Chamber of Sessions, June 22, 2011. - Deputy Antonio
Carlos Mendes Thame, PSDB/SP.

REQUEST No. 2.237, OF 2011
(From Mr. Luiz Alberto)
Requests the holding of a Solemn Session
in commemoration of the 58th (fifty-eight)
anniversary of Petrobras - October 3rd, to be held
on October 4, 2011 (Tuesday).
Mr. President,
In accordance with the rules, we request that
you take the necessary measures for the holding
of a Solemn Session in commemoration of the 58th
(fifty-eight) anniversary of Petrobras - October 3,
2011, to be held on October 4, 2011 (Tuesday).
Justification
Petrobras was founded on October 3, 1953, by
then-President of the Republic Getúlio Vargas, with
the objective of carrying out petroleum sector ac-
tivities in Brazil on behalf of the Union. "It is,
therefore, with satisfaction and patriotic pride that
I today sanction the text of the law approved by
the legislative power, which constitutes a new mar-
k in our economic independence," he had foreseen
over 50 years ago.
The creation of Petrobras is the result of a popu-
lar campaign that began in 1946, with the historic
slogan "Oil is ours."

Since its inception, Petrobras has always been driven by the challenge of providing energy capable of propelling development and securing society's future with competence, ethics, cordiality, and respect for diversity.
Petrobras represents a publicly held company, with the majority shareholder being the Brazilian Government, and operates as an energy company in the following sectors: exploration and production, refining, oil and natural gas marketing and transportation, petrochemicals, derivative distribution, electricity, biofuels, and other renewable energy sources.
As the leader in the Brazilian oil sector, it has expanded its operations to be among the top five integrated energy companies globally by 2020, and is currently present in 28 countries. Its Business Plan 2010-2014 foresees investments of US$224 billion.
As an integrated energy company, it operates in various fields. Its platforms search for oil in the depths of the ocean. With its refineries, it offers a variety of products that combine practicality, technology, and environmental respect.
In light of the above, we understand that holding this Solemn Session in the Chamber of Deputies' Plenary is a just tribute by the Brazilian Parliament to this Institution that represents one of our greatest National Treasures. And thus, this House reaffirms once again its recognition of the importance of this great Institution that has played a decisive role in our country's economic, social, cultural, and technological development.

REQUEST No. 2.253, OF 2011
(From Mr. Paes Landim)
Requests that the Law Project No. 3.405,
of 1997, be sent to the Finance and Taxation

Mr. President,
Decree No. 6.944, of 2009, establishes organizational
measures for the improvement of the direct federal
public administration, autonomous and foundation,
and also provides for general rules regarding public
conferences.
The normative seeks to strengthen institutional
capacity through the holding of public conferences
and the provision of public positions and jobs (article
1, § 2, item III) and clarifies the need for evaluation,
by the Ministry of Planning, Budget and Management,
of the proposals that deal with public conferences,
including the budgetary and financial impacts in the
exercise that should come into effect and in the
subsequent two exercises (article 5).
Due to the need to analyze these impacts,
the authorization for the holding of public conferences
and the decision on the provision of public positions
and jobs, as well as the issuance of the necessary
complementary acts, were delegated to the Minister
of State for Planning, Budget and Management (article
10).
Furthermore, as established by article 15 of the
mentioned legal instrument, it is up to the same
ministry to determine the amount charged for the
public conference registration, based on the estimated
costs indispensable for its holding.

This House is analyzing Bill No. 3,405 of 1997, which "provides for the provision of public note and record services, in accordance with Article 236, § 3 of the Federal Constitution."

Article 18 of the substitute approved by the Commission on Labor, Administration, and Public Service limits access to participants by privileging (in clauses II to VII) owners or employees of notarial offices. To give an idea, while the substitute (clause II of Article 18) grants (in the title proof) one point for each five-year period or fraction greater than thirty-six months to a candidate who has "delegation of notarial or record office service, considering, including, the period during which he or she served as designated responsible for the office of another service," it only attributes four-tenths for "each recognized doctoral or master's degree in Law" (clause XI), which appears as a disincentive for more qualified Brazilians to register for the competition.

Meanwhile, Article 2 of the substitute suggested in the Commission on Constitution and Justice and Citizenship, by amending Article 14 of Law No. 8,935 of November 18, 1994, establishes in its clause VIII the entry into the notarial activity of those who have exercised, for at least five years, the position of clerk in a notarial or record office.

In the same substitute, the contents of the competition tests are established, benefiting technical and administrative matters practiced by notaries (in the wording that confers to Article 15 of Law No. 8.935/94) and privileges the filling of vacancies, primarily, by removal of the current owners (who in some cases did not participate in public competitions) over the approved in the public competition for entry (wording given to Article 16 of the aforementioned Law).

Also in Article 18 of the substitute offered in the Commission on Constitution and Justice and Citizenship, there is a disincentive to the participation of Brazilians who do not have the delegation of notarial service ownership mentioned earlier in Article 18 of the substitute from the Commission on Labor, Administration, and Public Service.

By privileging notarial office holders, either as a requirement for participation in the competition, by forcing the tests to prioritize matters dealing with the daily activity of notaries, or by preference in filling vacancies for notaries, the bill inhibits the participation of Brazilians
DIARY OF THE HOUSE OF DEPUTIES

In the process and interferes in the evaluation, carried out by the Ministry of Planning, Budget and Management, of the proposals that deal with public contests, including the amount charged for registration from a smaller contingent of candidates among other budgetary-financial impacts.

Subsection "h" of Article 32, Item X, of the Internal Regulation of the Chamber of Deputies establishes as the responsibility of the Commission on Finance and Taxation to promote the evaluation of these impacts, as well as Article 54, Item II.

In light of the above, I request from Your Excellency, in accordance with the procedural rules indicated, that it be sent to the Commission on Finance and Taxation, in addition to the standing committees in the initial dispatch.

REQUEST NO. 2.255, OF 2011
(From Mr. Paes Landim)
Requests the redistribution of Bill No. 6,113, of 2009, authored by Senator Paulo Paim.
Mr. President,
I request, in accordance with Articles 140, 141 and 32, paragraph IV, subparagraphs “d”3 and “e”4 of the Internal Regulation, the redistribution of Bill No. 6,113, of 2009, which “amends the wording of Article 193 of the Consolidation of Labor Laws – CLT, approved by Decree-Law No. 5,452, of May 1st, 1943, to provide for hazardous activities or operations”, for analysis on the merits by the Committee on Constitution and Justice and Citizenship.
Justification
In accordance with the provisions of the aforementioned bill, the list of criteria for eligibility to receive the hazardous work additional would be significantly expanded, given the link between the additional and the worker's remuneration who performs a specific function under the risk of violating his/her physical integrity. See the highlighted excerpt of the proposed expression for the characterization of hazard in various types of labor activities:
“Hazardous activities or operations are those that, by their nature or work method, imply permanent contact with inflamables or explosives under conditions of heightened risk or exposure to a situation that puts life at risk, the imminent danger of an accident or physical violence.”
As provided by the relevant rules concerning the thematic areas covered by the Committee on Constitution and Justice and Citizenship, proposals that deal with fundamental rights and guarantees, or that deal with matters concerning constitutional law (subparagraphs “d” and “e”, paragraph IV, Article 32) are subject to merit examination by the Committee. In short, the compliance with these regulatory requirements places the Committee on Constitution and Justice and Citizenship among the actors in the legislative process that have the competence to judge the merits of Bill No. 6,113, of 2009, due to the fact that it deals with the fundamental guarantee to physical integrity.

The Federal Constitution of 1988 does not explicitly provide for the guarantee or protection of bodily integrity. However, this is addressed by Article 5, § 2 of the Constitution, which states that "the rights and guarantees expressed in this Constitution do not exclude others deriving from the regime and principles it adopts, or from international treaties in which the Federative Republic of Brazil is a party."

International conventions that Brazil is a signatory to thus serve as sources of individual and collective rights. Specifically, the American Convention on Human Rights (Pact of San José de Costa Rica) establishes in its Article 5 the right to personal integrity, whereby every person has the right for their physical, mental, and moral integrity to be respected.

In summary, Article 5 of the American Convention on Human Rights, complementing the Constitution, under the force of Article 5, § 2, explicitly ensures the unrestricted and effective protection of bodily integrity, which is in force in the Brazilian legal system as a fundamental right guaranteed by constitutional legislation.

It is also relevant to note that, under the chairmanship of Honorable Deputy Nelson Pellegrino, within the Committee on Constitution and Justice and Citizenship, the Legislative Project No. 6,113 of 2009 received a report highlighting that the examined text, due to not meeting the requirements of legality and good legislative technique, required amendments from the Committee. This understanding led the rapporteur to present a substitute amendment, but the desk procedure carried out by the House's Directorate, which did not include the CCJC's merit review, made it impossible to rectify the aforementioned defects, prompting the rapporteur to present a second report that does not include corrections to the Senate Federal Legislative Project.

These are the arguments that demonstrate the Committee's competence to express its opinion on the merits of the proposal.

Therefore, based on the provisions of Article 32, IV, alines "d" and "e" of this House's Internal Regulation, I request from Your Excellency the redistribution of Legislative Project No. 6,113 of 2009, which "amends the wording of Article 193 of the Consolidated Laws of Work - CLT, approved by Decree-Law No. 5,452 of May 1st, 1943, to provide for hazardous activities or operations," for merit analysis in the Committee on Constitution and Justice and Citizenship.

The floor is given to Mr. Deputy Paes Landim, on behalf of the

MR. PAES LANDIM (Parliamentary Block/PTB-PI.) – Mr. President, the competent journalist from my state, Cláudio Barros, in his column Frente Ampla, initiated an important debate regarding the creation of a new state in the Piauí territory, which would initially be named Estado do Gurgueia. He presents here the testimony of one of the most serious individuals in my state, one of the best figures of the new generation of Piauí economists, Dr. Sérgio Miranda, the current Secretary of Planning of Piauí and who was also part of the previous government. Sérgio is a grateful revelation, a serious young man. He states that he disagrees with the columnist regarding the absence of an economic base for the creation of a new state in Piauí, as he sees that the region where it is intended to create the new state has a very strong economic base, based mainly on agribusiness and mining. I would also mention the exuberance of its natural beauty, its parks and rivers, if they are duly preserved, due to the wealth that results from them.

Sérgio Miranda agrees that “the division may be a Greek gift to what remains of Piauí, with a worsening of the ratio between long-term debt and current liquid revenue.”

He continues:

“And not only the debt and revenue aspects, but the entire structure of public finances of what will be Piauí will suffer a huge blow, since a large part of the expenditure on personnel structure (including social security) will fall on the shoulders of the Piauians. Gurgueia will be born light and healthy, while Piauí will bear practically the same current weight, with smaller revenues.”

Mr. President, here Dr. Sérgio Miranda gives us exactly one of the best justifications for the creation of the new state. The bloated structure of public administration in Piauí, centered in Teresina, at the expense of the rest of the state, is one of the reasons why the south of Piauí is neglected, especially its extreme south.

It is now evident that cities the size of Corrente have two judge positions – cities like Gilbués

– And they've been without magistrates for a long time, to give an example from the far south.

Now, the state electricity company, before being federalized, CEPISA, had, at one time, more doctors than engineers in the State Capital of Piauí. Look at the abuses that the political elite of Piauí concentrated in Teresina, where, of course, the best families of the state, including families linked to those who held power, reside. The creation of the new state would have long required the establishment of a local administrative structure to leverage its potential wealth and prevent the death of its rivers, Parnaíba, Gurgueia (the contract is already dead), the Piauí River itself, and several others. It would also have spared its forest, fauna, flora, and its rich biodiversity of the Cerrado. In short, either we will soon have a local government nearby, or, Mr. President, a great desert announces itself there for the next 20 years, due to a lack of a conscious environmental policy for the defense of the future state. We would preserve the great environmental parks of Serra da Capivara and Serra das Confusões and the Nascentes, where the Parnaíba River is born, which has not yet been implemented, and also the environmental area around Serra Vermelha.

Mr. President, Dr. Sérgio is also concerned that the creation of the new state of Gurgueia may have a negative impact on the lives of the Piauienses who will be on this side. I don't think so. On the contrary, there will be constitutional resources practically of the same size that will be applied in a smaller space than the current Piauí.

By the way, Mr. President, regarding the name of the state, a few days ago, in the city of São Raimundo Nonato, I met a citizen who said something interesting: "Deputy, I am in favor of the new state, I am passionate, but why not keep the name Piauí? If our Piauí River is born here, why not Piauí do Sul?" I found this approach interesting. It is still possible to change it, depending on a consultation, of course. The change could be made through a drafting amendment when the project is on the agenda here in the plenary, since it has already been approved by all committees of this House.

Mr. President, a few days ago, I also read an opinion very interesting from a State Deputy from Piauí against the creation of the state of Gurgueia. His opinion makes sense. He asks the IPEA to conduct a study on the future state.

I have said it many times before that, until we show the federal government our potential and that we may be the new Tocantins or even richer than Tocantins with lower costs, since we have cities with structures...

The paintings are enough to establish a new capital,
which Tocantins did not have...
The IPEA is a qualified body, because for several years
I have been trying to get the State Government to pay
the Getúlio Vargas Foundation to conduct this study,
to show feasibility, to demonstrate the great potential
wealth of the future state. It's clear that the constitu-
tional costs are enormous. We are not to blame.
Unfortunately, the Federal Constitution requires—and
it's exactly a petrified clause—a minimum of eight
legislators per state, which I consider absurd. We
need to change the entire constitutional text. This
can only be done through a constituent process
convened for this purpose to correct these distortions
that are not our fault.
A few days ago, Folha de S.Paulo made an important
comment. With the creation of new states, there
would be a great imbalance between the banks of
the Northeast and the South of the country.
It is true that in a federation, the great balance is
the Senate. This is the great lesson of the Americans.
But even so, we have distortions in our representative
system that does not accurately represent the
state's population. This was a maneuver of the
authoritarian regime in the 1970s, when exactly
the electorate, not the population, determined the
representative numbers of the states.
But the Senate is the balance point. If we could
correct some deficiencies constitutionally that
could result in cost increases!
But the fact is that our state, unlike Tocantins,
which already had international resources allocated
to the future state, paid for by the Union as guarantor,
did not even have access to PRODECER.
The only cerrado in Brazil that did not have access
to the Japanese Cerrado Development Program
was that of Piauí.
So, we have the conditions to have a rationalized,
balanced state that would bring few costs for its
implementation and would immediately bring the
Union solid resources, increased export value, and
high productivity in its economy, given that its
area is entirely included in the Transnordestina
railway.
The extreme south is neglected. Our borders are
unguarded. Bahia is advancing into our territory.
Even Tocantins is advancing into the full Mangabeira
Mountain Range due to the absence of the Piauí
state.
Therefore, only through a great insensitivity
could we, at this moment, disagree with the creation
of the new state, which would bring more wealth to
Piauí, more social welfare, including improving
health and education indicators.

For example, Mr. President, the Corrente Hospital in Piauí, the state's gateway, was recently opened after being closed for a lack of an X-ray machine. In Tocantins, there was no city like Corrente when it became a state. Just 180 kilometers from Barreiras, Bahia, a significant portion of medical care for our compatriots in the southern extreme of Piauí State is provided there, given the nearly 900-kilometer distance to Teresina. Only the creation of a new state could harness the immense potential there, or we risk having, in 20 years, a vast desert due to abandonment and the lack of a local government. Thank you, Mr. President.

DEPUTY JAIME MARTINS (Bloc/PR-MG, in order, without revision) – Mr. President, I would like, in greeting all those listening, to refer to the VIII High Studies Notebook that we recently launched, titled "Mineral Sector: Towards a New Legal Framework."

For another year, we have been working with consultants from this House to develop a proposal that could become the new regulatory framework for Brazil's mineral sector.

I believe this House and the Government, in general, cannot further delay the debate on this important topic for both the present and future generations.

I would like to emphasize that this Notebook consolidates the studies prepared within the Legislative Consulting Office, as we mentioned, and also the contributions from participants in a seminar held in the Chamber of Deputies' TV auditorium last December, when this topic of mining activity was discussed.

The publication includes a detailed and plural analysis of the current regulatory model for this sector, which highlighted the general view that changes are needed to establish a new and modern legal relationship between the Brazilian State and the economic agents who exploit this activity.

Thank you, Mr. President.

segments.text:
Launch of the VIII High-Level Study Book, titled
Mineral Sector: Towards a New Legal Landmark.
Under my guidance, this Book consolidates the
studies carried out within the Legislative Consulting
and the contributions of participants in a seminar
held in the TV Câmara auditorium last December,
where a new legal framework for mining activities
was discussed.
The publication includes a detailed and plural
analysis of the current regulatory model for this sector,
which highlighted the general view that changes are
needed to establish a new and modern legal relation
between the Brazilian State and economic agents.
For this new relation to be effective, it is essential
that institutional changes take place. In this regard,
we have drafted Indication No. 2012/2008, suggesting
to the Honorable President of the Republic the
establishment of the National Mineral Resources
Agency, the creation of the National Mineral Policy
Council, and the strengthening of the Brazilian
Geological Service.
Regarding constitutional aspects, the 1988 Political
Charter established that mineral resources are federal
property, and included the exploration of these
resources under the State's full guardianship. Article
176 contains an expression that should guide all
legislation: the "national interest," according to
which the exploration and extraction of mineral
resources should take place.
Article 176 also stipulates that the exploration and
extraction of mineral resources can only be carried
out with the authorization or concession of the Union.
While ensuring State control over the mineral
patrimony, it defines who is responsible for carrying
out mining activities. It reflects the State's interest
in guaranteeing sovereignty over the mineralized
soil and subsoil, and the importance of private law
entities in the production of mineral goods.
In our view, the terms "authorization" and
"concession" should be understood as the classical
institutes of Administrative Law, used, for example,
in the exploitation of hydraulic energy potential.
Thus, it can be argued that the current Mining Code
would not have been received by the Federal
Constitution.
It is therefore necessary to adapt this Code to
the new state design promoted by the 1988 Federal
Constitution. This is the main objective of Project
of Law No. 463/2011, authored by members of the
High-Level Study and Technological Assessment
Council.
The mineral concession should be a sovereign
act of political power, characterized as a public
law contract. Our conclusion is that this modality
should be classified as...
DIARY OF THE HOUSE OF DEPUTIES

As a concession of public asset, to be granted through an administrative contract.

A curious aspect of this topic is the argument that subjecting mineral entrepreneurs to an administrative contract would create legal uncertainty. This is particularly curious because concessions provide the highest level of legal security for individuals dealing with the public administration.

Another important conclusion relates to the factual situation of many interested parties seeking to explore a particular area. In such cases, the state should promote a competitive bidding process, treating all interested parties equally.

According to current procedures, competition occurs on a non-equal basis, which is unconstitutional. Preference is given to the first party to submit a research request. The allocation of the area to the first arrival, even if other entrepreneurs manifest interest, is due to what is known as the right of priority.

When competition is feasible, we consider that the right of priority becomes incompatible with the principle of equality and, therefore, materially unconstitutional. The privilege of chronological order over technical aspects makes this institution obsolete, un-republican, and incompatible with the model of state designed by the 1988 Constitution.

Once the mineral research is granted and carried out, we propose that the subsequent step, the concession or authorization of mining, should also be conducted through a competitive process. One alternative to be evaluated by the legislator is that in which the researcher, once the activities specified in the research authorization are completed, and even if their participation in this stage of the process is over, can compete with other interested parties in the subsequent stage.

If the researcher does not win the bidding process for the authorization or mining concession, they, who have completed the activities specified in the research authorization, would have a share in the mining result.

Regarding investments in mineral exploration, according to DNPM data, they have shown significant growth.

Despite this growth, the resources allocated to mineral research in Brazil can still be considered very modest.

Mining companies have preferred to keep their research programs limited to their own mines and expand their activities by acquiring third-party deposits.

The North American countries, consisting of Canada, the United States, and Mexico, have been the preferred destinations for investors, accounting for nearly one-third of global investment. Latin America, excluding Mexico, ranks second. Brazil receives only approximately 10% of regional investments. Regarding taxation, several studies on the mining sector demonstrate that, although Brazil's tax model may be improved, particularly in terms of the number of taxes, it does not confer a competitive disadvantage to the sector.

In a 2007 study by the International Monetary Fund, Brazil was the country with the lowest state share in the total benefits from iron ore projects. Among the countries analyzed was Australia.

In Brazil in 2010, oil and natural gas production generated royalties and special participations totaling R$ 21 billion. It is important to clarify that the special participation, which is a special royalty, constitutes an extraordinary financial compensation due by oil or natural gas exploration and production concessionaires in cases of high production volume or significant profitability.

In the mining sector, where there is no special participation, the financial compensation collected in 2010 was only R$ 1.2 billion.

Despite the significant difference between the oil sector and the mining sector, a difference in financial compensation collection of such magnitude does not seem justified.

We therefore propose the creation of a special participation in the mining sector, which would only affect large deposits or high-profitability deposits, thereby increasing the Union, states, and municipalities' share of mining revenue.

With the aim of establishing this participation, the aforementioned Bill No. 463 of 2011, in addition to amending the Mining Code, modifies Law No. 8,001 of 1990.

It is also important to note that there are no incentives for value addition to Brazilian mineral resources. The Kandir Law and the lack of export tax collection favor the export of products from the mineral extraction industry.

In our view, this law should be amended to subject exports of non-renewable primary products to ICMS. In this regard, we have presented Complementary Bill No. 11 of 2011, which is also currently under consideration.

Given the relevance and complexity of this fascinating topic, we are certain that this VIII Notebook can contribute to the Legislative Power's adoption of appropriate measures.
DIARY OF THE HOUSE OF DEPUTIES

the interests of the Brazilian population.

thorities from hiring companies whose partners are de-
puties or relatives up to the third degree.
Unfortunately, I was unable to get it passed in that
house.
In the previous term, here in the Chamber of Depu-
ties, I had the opportunity to present the same bill. Since
I was serving in the Secretariat, I did not follow its pro-
gression very closely. It went through this House, and
here it may have lost its essence, because the bill deals
with prohibiting the hiring and even the conclusion of
agreements with institutions and companies. In this
House, they removed the terms "contract" and "hiring,"
leaving only "agreements." I am now working to change
that, to retrieve the term "contracts" in the Senate, be-
cause I believe this is a relevant issue, and this House
needs to take these measures so that the executive, par-
ticularly, does not hire companies linked to authorities.

The most serious thing that has been happening, Mr.
President, is that most of the contracts are being made
in the form of emergency contracts, that is, they do not
even participate in bidding processes. Today's article
says that for these companies linked to deputies, 773 mil-
lion reais were paid. Just this year, 2011, almost 80 mil-
lion reais were paid to companies linked to deputies. And
many of these contracts are emergency contracts.

The information I have is that this project was transformed into a recommendation, having been sent to the Executive to then forward to the Chamber a similar project. Happens, Mr. President, that this same project deals with agreements, that is, it also prohibits the hiring of NGOs linked to authorities. I recently sent a request to the Ministry of Sports and the Ministry of Justice, requesting releases of resources. I became aware of over 2 million reais just for one entity, a NGO from Sobradinho called Cata-Ventos, linked precisely to a former District Deputy, now Federal Deputy, currently Secretary of Government of the Federal District. This entity had a project of its initiative approved in the Legislative Assembly as a relevant entity of public utility. Shortly after, when he was still Minister of Sports, Governor Agnelo released millions of resources to this entity, not only for it, but for several other NGOs in the Federal District. I requested, and already received, the approval of the Desk for the requests I made. I want to lift all the resources that were transferred to these entities, mainly to Cata-Ventos. They are resources from the Second Time Program. I do not know if Mr. Deputy Ribamar Alves, knows, in Maranhão or in other states, the Second Time, which is a wonderful project. It takes children off the streets and gives opportunity to poor children to practice sports. The Government hires monitors, physical education teachers, encouraging sport mainly in the most deprived areas. Unfortunately, the Federal District has been prejudiced with these projects. We already had a big problem here with the Fund for the Assistance to the Worker. For many years, the Federal District has not received resources from the FAT, precisely due to a lack of credibility and resource diversions that were made here during some administrations. Now the same is happening with the Second Time. For a long time, the institutions of the Federal District have not been receiving resources precisely because they do not apply these resources correctly to these entities.

A project like this, which was voted yesterday in the CCJ of the Legislative Assembly and was archived, transformed into a recommendation! I doubt very much, especially with this participation of NGOs, that the Governor will forward to the Legislative Assembly an Executive project dealing with this matter. Perhaps he was the biggest encourager of the application of resources in phantom NGOs, as denounced in the magazines Veja, ISTOÉ and Época: resource diversion, with accounting of fake invoices from Novo Ho-
DIARY OF THE HOUSE OF DEPUTIES

The horizon, with testimony from people who received resources - there are many testimonies on this matter. I deeply regret that this bill was not approved. But I am sure that we will be able to rescue the essence of the project in the Senate, which is the prohibition of contracting companies of Deputies and relatives, while also maintaining the issue of agreements to preserve the prohibition of repassings to non-governmental entities that have actually received the resources and not applied them correctly.

So, we are working with Senators to rescue this, because it will return to the Chamber, and here I am sure we will be able to convince Deputies that, much more than legal, this is a moral, ethical issue. It is not acceptable for companies of Parliamentarians, companies of authorities linked to the Government, to provide services for the Government itself. This really goes against transparency, the ethics of public service.

So, I want to appeal to the Members of Parliament to give us a lot of strength regarding this project, so that this House can approve it and, thus, definitively prohibit, both in Municipalities, as well as in Governments, in Court of Accounts, in the Legislative itself, that Deputies and their relatives have this privilege of being contracted, even without public bidding, through emergency contracts.

That's all, Mr. President. Thank you very much.

According to Luiz Aubert – and this is the crucial point of everything we refer to today: "Brazil is not competitive", mentioning the exchange rate policy that keeps the real valued, the high interest rates, the infamous "Custo Brasil" (Brazil's cost) and the country's high tax burden. "Brazil is not competitive." He has reasons to say that and we will return to this sentence.
The Brazilian Institute of Economy of the Getúlio Vargas Foundation, in a letter titled The Brazilian Deindustrialization Debate, argues that the industrial sector of the Brazilian economy is facing a moment of deindustrialization, for which many economists have frequently drawn attention in their analyses.
The main causes of this distrust, according to the Getúlio Vargas Foundation, are the real's appreciation, the global financial crisis and the "China effect", in reference to that Asian country's bet on emerging countries and specifically the case of competition with Brazilian products, often unfair, of their manufactured products with ours.
The letter comments that "in the light of international experience, until 2008, the process of deindustrialization in Brazil would be occurring within the standard." In fact, the share of imported industrialized products in the Brazilian market is increasing, and our export volume is falling, but in a bearable way until 2008. However, look what is happening today: excluding vehicles, it is 25% lower than three years ago. What is 25% lower? The volume of Brazilian exports.
In the last 8 years in Brazil, retail sales have grown more than industry in every year. If retail sales grow more than industry, how do we meet this demand? Through an increase in imports.
Meanwhile, the volume of Brazilian exports to the United States, our main external destination for manufactured goods, was, last year, 36% lower than the period prior to the crisis initiated in 2008. It is possible that the phenomenon is attributable to the contraction of the US economy. Our exports to Japan and Europe have also not yet recovered.
DIARY OF THE HOUSE OF DEPUTIES

They returned to pre-crisis levels, reflecting a brutal
consumption contraction there and a strong expansion here, leading our industry and theirs to redirect products to the Brazilian domestic market.
Meanwhile, our exports to China—the world's fastest-growing country and the main importer of our raw materials (raw materials!)—increased by 77% just in quantity since the crisis, not to mention the price gains.
However, in recent years, the growth of our exports has resulted in a much more restricted spread of technical progress, as in the case of agriculture, livestock, and even more so in mining, than would have been possible if Brazilian manufactured exports had grown or maintained their previous share of Brazil's trade balance. And this is due to the effects of spillover and the way technical progress is assimilated in primary sectors. In other words, the productivity gains are much smaller in these sectors.
For example, what happens in a segment of fine chemicals, the result of technology developed outside the country, such as modern agricultural inputs, more modern fertilizers, more efficient seeds, more efficient genetic matrices, all much more linked to agriculture and livestock than to the industrial economic sector, and highly dependent on international monopolies.
The effects are sectorially more contained than those of technological advancement when it occurs in the industrial sector that permeates everything, spreading to segments of the service sector, requiring better education of the workforce, better engineering services, more technologically advanced urban equipment, better training and capacitation of employed labor.
However, many end up blaming the sector itself, saying it's a "deindustrialization of Brazil," characterized by the technological depletion of productive chains. And that's exactly what we want to contest—contest with the words of President Luiz Aubert of ABIMAQ: "Brazil is not competitive." It's not the industry that's not competitive. It ends up becoming non-competitive due to issues linked to Brazil as a whole, such as the overvalued real, high interest rates, super-deficient infrastructure that hasn't kept pace with industrial sector development, in short, the infamous "cost of Brazil," in addition to the very high tax burden in Brazil. That's what's holding it back; that's what's the real Brazilian disease, not the disease of the Brazilian industry.

With these data, we witness in Brazil a long march back to the past, a return to a primary, export-oriented past from the times before the Round Table.
It is up to us to do everything possible to avoid this brutal setback, which destroys jobs and the well-being of all Brazilians.

MR. OSMAR TERRA (PMDB-RS. In order. Without a speaker’s review.) – Mr. President, Ladies and Gentlemen Deputies, I would like to speak once again on a recurring topic: drugs, which are proliferating in the country.
I have seen, with great sorrow, recent photos and accounts on this issue. Our Special Commission on Public Policy and the Fight Against Drugs visited the cracolândia in the city of São Paulo. The cracolândias, which are scattered throughout the country, are in fact the tip of the iceberg.
I have information that the National Secretariat for Drug Policy is conducting research on cracolândias, but it is impossible to get an idea or obtain real data on the situation of crack and drugs in Brazil just from the cracolândias – they are the tip of the iceberg. However, from the cracolândias, we can infer how the rest of the country is doing.
It is unacceptable that the Federal, state, or municipal governments – I am not speaking with any partisan bias – allow that horrifying, sad spectacle of human decay to take place in the center of São Paulo. There are thousands of people using drugs all the time, without any response from the government, without the government taking any action.
It is deplorable, Mr. President. As a Brazilian, a doctor, and a person interested in public health, I regret that that is allowed to happen, as it is. By the way, with the creation of a field, in the name of whatever – it cannot be in the name of human rights – for free use of drugs, the worst ones that can be used in Brazil.
I believe that Rio de Janeiro has shown the way and is taking action. São Paulo needs to act. Rio de Janeiro is taking children and a

I had the opportunity to participate in the Narcotics
